title: Coroutine Exception Handling
scopeHtml: Scope: how exceptions travel through the Job tree (launch vs async, root vs child), CoroutineExceptionHandler rules, supervisor scopes, aggregation, CancellationException's special status, Android crash behavior, and ViewModel/Result-type error strategies. Cancellation mechanics are in C5, flow catch/retry is in F6.

notes.title: launch versus async propagation
notes.html:
The idea, simply. There are two kinds of coroutine builders when it comes to errors. launch is "fire and forget": if it breaks, it shouts immediately to its boss (the parent / the app). async is "bring me a result": it keeps the exception inside the Deferred and throws it when you call await(). But there is a catch: if async has a parent, it also tells the parent right away.

Builder Where the exception goes
launch (child of a scope/coroutine) Immediately cancels the parent (failure goes up). Reaches the root and the handler/crash
launch (root: directly in a scope with no failing parent above, e.g. viewModelScope) The root passes it to CoroutineExceptionHandler, else the thread's uncaught handler (crash on Android)
async as a root (parent is a supervisor or it has no failing parent) Stored in the Deferred; thrown by await(). If you never await, nobody sees it
async as a child in a normal scope Cancels the parent immediately AND is thrown on await() 
viewModelScope.launch {
    val a = async { api.a() }      // child of the launch coroutine
    val b = async { api.b() }
    try { a.await() } catch (e: IOException) { /* too late: parent is already cancelled */ }
}

Common surprise. A try/catch around await() does not save the parent when async is a child in a regular scope: the failure already went up. To really contain it, wrap in supervisorScope { } or put the try/catch inside the async block.

Industry examples. Parallel loading of a profile + feed + notifications in Instagram-like home screens (async pairs inside coroutineScope); Swiggy-style checkout loading cart, address and offers in parallel and choosing per-call fallbacks.

Real-life picture. launch is an employee who runs into the boss's office the moment something breaks; async is one who writes a report and hands it over when asked (but if a manager is in the room, the manager hears the crash too).

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking try { async { ... } } catch catches the exception (the exception arises at await).
  • Never calling await() on a root async and losing the error.
  • Forgetting that a child async also fails its parent.

notes.title: try catch around launch and coroutineScope rethrow
notes.html:
The classic mistake. Wrapping launch in try/catch catches nothing: launch returns immediately, the work happens later in another coroutine.

try {
    scope.launch { throw IOException() }   // returns at once; exception is NOT caught here
} catch (e: IOException) { /* never runs */ }

scope.launch {
    try { throw IOException() } catch (e: IOException) { /* works: catch inside */ }
}

coroutineScope and withContext rethrow. These are suspend functions that finish only when their block does, so the exception is thrown to the caller where try/catch works:

try {
    coroutineScope { launch { throw IOException() } }   // rethrown here
} catch (e: IOException) { handle(e) }

Details: coroutineScope's child failure first cancels siblings; then the original exception is rethrown after all children finish. withContext rethrows the block's exception (stack trace may be recovered/copied in debug mode with the original as cause). That's why repository code like suspend fun load() = withContext(io) { api.get() } lets the ViewModel use plain try/catch.

Industry example. Retrofit suspend functions throw HttpException/IOException directly to the caller; ViewModels wrap them in try/catch or in Result.

Real-life picture. Posting a letter does not tell you whether the other person liked it; a phone call (suspend) lets you hear the reaction immediately.

Common interview traps.

  • try/catch around launch/async builder calls.
  • Thinking coroutineScope swallows child exceptions.
  • Catching in coroutineScope but expecting siblings to continue (they are cancelled).

notes.title: Uncaught exceptions crash Android
notes.html:
What happens. If an exception reaches a root coroutine and no CoroutineExceptionHandler handles it, kotlinx.coroutines passes it to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler (and to platform handlers; on Android it also uses an Android pre-handler path, confirm details in your coroutines version). On Android the default handler kills the process: users see "App has stopped" and Crashlytics logs a fatal crash, usually with the coroutine's stack trace.

Why viewModelScope still crashes. viewModelScope uses SupervisorJob, which prevents failures cancelling siblings, but does not catch them. A throwing viewModelScope.launch crashes the app unless you catch it or install a handler.

Where it shows up.

  • A NullPointerException, IllegalStateException or HttpException thrown by a launch in a ViewModel.
  • Exceptions in launch on Dispatchers.Default crash the same way, from DefaultDispatcher-worker-N.
  • In production Crashlytics shows kotlinx.coroutines.internal.DiagnosticCoroutineContextException (an attached suppressed exception carrying the coroutine context) in newer versions.

Industry practice. Apps like Spotify/Uber use their own scope wrappers that install a handler to log to Crashlytics and show a generic error, but only for non-programmer errors; programmer errors should still crash in debug.

Real-life picture. An unhandled shout at a factory sets off the whole fire alarm.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking SupervisorJob prevents crashes.
  • Assuming exceptions in background dispatchers do not crash the app.
  • Using a handler to hide real bugs.

notes.title: CoroutineExceptionHandler where it works
notes.html:
What it is. A context element called as the last resort for exceptions nobody caught in a coroutine tree. It logs/reports; it cannot recover or resume: the coroutine is already cancelled when the handler is called.

val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.e("App", "boom", e) }
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main + handler)
scope.launch { throw IllegalStateException() }   // handler called

It only works on a root coroutine. A "root" is a coroutine with no parent that will handle the failure: scope.launch(handler), children of a SupervisorJob/supervisorScope, GlobalScope. A handler set on a child launch of a normal parent is ignored because the exception is passed up, and only the root's handler (the one in the root's context) is consulted.

scope.launch {                         // root (no handler here)
    launch(handler) { throw E() }      // handler IGNORED: child passes failure to parent
}
scope.launch(handler) { launch { throw E() } }    // works: handler on the root

async ignores it. A root async stores the exception in the Deferred; the handler is never called (even when never awaited). A child of a normal scope reports to the parent.

With supervisorScope. Children of supervisorScope are roots for exception purposes: each can have its own handler, or inherit the one in the surrounding context (handlers installed in the supervisorScope block's context are inherited by its children). supervisorScope itself rethrows the block's exception, not the children's.

Misplaced handler (spot-the-bug). Passing the handler to withContext(handler), coroutineScope, or a nested launch does nothing; install it on the scope or the root launch.

Retry inside a handler (incident). Code like CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, _ -> scope.launch { fetch() } } to "retry on failure": the failed coroutine is already dead; the retry runs in a new coroutine that can fail the same way, causing infinite crash loops, hammering the server and draining battery. Do retries inside the coroutine with retry/exponential backoff (and a cap) and treat the handler only as logging.

Industry examples. Application-wide scope handlers sending to Crashlytics/Sentry; Ktor's CallLogging.

Real-life picture. A hospital's incident report form: it gets filled after something went wrong; it cannot undo what happened.

Common interview traps.

  • Handler on a child coroutine (ignored).
  • Expecting it to catch async exceptions.
  • Trying to recover or retry from the handler.
  • Forgetting CancellationException never reaches it.

notes.title: CancellationException is special
notes.html:
Behaviour in exception handling.

  • A coroutine cancelled with CancellationException is considered a normal cancellation: not passed to a handler, does not crash, does not cancel the parent.
  • If any other exception occurs while cancelling, that becomes the failure.
  • catch (e: Exception) swallows it (see the cancellation notes).

Awaiting a Deferred cancelled elsewhere (production incident). Coroutine A calls deferredB.await(). Another coroutine cancels B (for instance refreshJob.cancel() on a new refresh). await() throws CancellationException in A, even though A itself was not cancelled. A treats it as its own cancellation and the exception unwinds silently: the screen never shows data or error ("infinite spinner", no crash, no log). Handle it: catch CancellationException, then ensureActive() (rethrows only if A itself is cancelled), otherwise treat as "result missing" and retry or show an error. Or avoid sharing a cancellable Deferred between consumers, using shareIn/stateIn or a Mutex-guarded single-flight job instead.

Real-life picture. A waiter told "table 5 cancelled" quietly leaves, not realising the whole restaurant is still open.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a cancelled await means the awaiting coroutine was cancelled.
  • Catching all exceptions around await and forgetting ensureActive.
  • Expecting CEH to log cancellations.

notes.title: Aggregated and suppressed exceptions
notes.html:
The idea. When many children of one scope fail at nearly the same time, only one exception can be "the" failure: the first one is the root cause and wins; later ones are attached as suppressed exceptions (Throwable.addSuppressed).

try {
    coroutineScope {
        launch { throw IOException("A") }
        launch { throw IllegalStateException("B") }
    }
} catch (e: Exception) {
    e.message                 // "A" (first)
    e.suppressed.toList()     // [IllegalStateException B] (maybe)
}

Important details:

  • Which child "wins" depends on scheduling; don't rely on it.
  • A CancellationException caused by sibling cancellation is not added as suppressed noise.
  • Exceptions thrown from finally while another exception is in flight become suppressed on the original (so logs may show the cleanup failure only in the "Suppressed:" section; make sure your logging prints them: Crashlytics does).
  • In debug mode, stack trace recovery copies exceptions to add the caller stack; the original is the cause.

Industry example. Parallel uploads (photo backup) where 20 fail on server validation: you log first + suppressed count, but for user-level reporting collect per-item results.

Real-life picture. Several fire alarms ring at once; the first one is written in the log as "the" incident, others as notes.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming all exceptions are reported separately.
  • Ignoring suppressed when debugging.
  • Expecting deterministic first exception.

notes.title: Exceptions thrown while handling exceptions
notes.html:
The rules.

  • If the CoroutineExceptionHandler itself throws, that exception goes to the thread's uncaught handler (crash), and the original exception is added as suppressed to it where possible. A buggy logging handler can crash the app even though the original error was "handled".
  • Exceptions in finally/use {} close() while another is propagating are attached as suppressed.
  • Exceptions from invokeOnCompletion handlers are wrapped in CompletionHandlerException and reported to the uncaught handler.
  • Exceptions thrown inside onCancellation/onUndeliveredElement lambdas are also wrapped and delivered as uncaught.

Defensive rule. Keep handlers tiny: log, report, never do IO or throw. Wrap risky logging in try/catch.

Real-life picture. The smoke detector's battery dies while it is beeping about a fire.

Common interview traps.

  • Handler code that can throw (null pointers in a logger).
  • Believing exceptions in finally replace the original silently (they are suppressed on it).

notes.title: Observing failure from outside
notes.html:
Ways to see a coroutine's outcome without catching inside.

  • job.invokeOnCompletion { cause -> ... }: cause is null on success, a CancellationException on cancel, or the failure. Runs once on a thread that completes the job (keep it non-blocking).
  • job.join(): does not throw the failure for launch jobs (join just waits); failure goes via the parent/handler.
  • deferred.await() rethrows the failure.
  • deferred.getCompletionExceptionOrNull() is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi; use only if allowed.
  • Flow: flow.catch { }, onCompletion { cause -> }.
  • CoroutineExceptionHandler for reporting.
val job = scope.launch { risky() }
job.invokeOnCompletion { cause ->
    if (cause != null && cause !is CancellationException) analytics.log(cause)
}

Industry example. Analytics wrappers log "task failed" with invokeOnCompletion so every coroutine reports without try/catch clutter.

Real-life picture. A delivery tracking SMS that arrives after the parcel is delivered or lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting join() to throw.
  • Doing heavy work in invokeOnCompletion.
  • Counting cancellation as failure in analytics.

notes.title: What to catch
notes.html:
Rule. Catch the narrowest type you can handle, and never swallow cancellation.

Catch Problem
Throwable also catches OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, CancellationException and bugs
Exception still catches CancellationException and programmer errors (NPE, IllegalState)
IOException, HttpException, SerializationException what you can actually handle

For network code: IOException means no connectivity/timeouts (retryable); HttpException 4xx/5xx (map by code); parse errors are bugs or contract changes (report). Programmer errors (NPE, IllegalArgumentException) should crash in debug and get reported in release instead of being "handled" into silent empty screens. If you must catch broadly (a top-level boundary), rethrow CancellationException and log everything else.

Real-life picture. A doctor treating a fever with a fever medicine, not with "whatever is in the cupboard".

Common interview traps.

  • catch (e: Throwable) around suspend calls.
  • Catching Exception and turning bugs into "Something went wrong".
  • Catching broad type without rethrowing CancellationException.

notes.title: ViewModel error strategies and Result types
notes.html:
Strategies in a ViewModel.

  1. try/catch inside viewModelScope.launch, update UI state with an error. Simple, explicit.
  2. Return a Result/sealed type from the repository and let the ViewModel branch. Failures become values, forcing handling at compile time.
  3. Flow .catch { emit(UiState.Error) } for streams.
  4. A handler on the scope for unexpected failures only (log/report).
  5. Single-event channel for one-off error messages (snackbar).
sealed interface UiState { data object Loading : UiState; data class Data(val x: X) : UiState; data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState }
viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.value = try { UiState.Data(repo.load()) }
    catch (e: IOException) { UiState.Error("No connection") }
}

Exceptions vs Result types. Kotlin's built-in Result/runCatching is easy but (a) runCatching catches CancellationException (bug in suspend code), (b) it is not designed as a public API return type (before Kotlin 1.5 it was restricted). Many teams use custom sealed Outcome<T> or Arrow's Either. Use exceptions for exceptional/unexpected failures and cancellation; Results for expected, user-visible outcomes (invalid card, not found).

launchSafe wrapper (post-incident). A team added fun CoroutineScope.launchSafe(block) = launch { try { block() } catch (e: Exception) { log(e) } }. Problems found: it swallowed CancellationException (zombie work after screen exit, battery drain), hid programmer errors (no crash, silent empty screens), and also hid the failure from the UI (no error state). Fix: rethrow cancellation, report to Crashlytics as non-fatal, expose an error state/callback, let programmer errors crash in debug.

Industry examples. Now in Android uses Result-like sealed classes (Result.Loading/Success/Error) and .catch on flows; Google Pay-style flows use sealed outcomes for declined payments.

Real-life picture. A restaurant order slip that states "out of stock" (a value) versus a kitchen fire (an exception).

Common interview traps.

  • runCatching in suspend code.
  • A generic safe-launch helper that swallows errors and cancellation.
  • Using exceptions for normal control flow like "not found".

notes.title: Dead scope after the first failure
notes.html:
The problem. A scope built with a plain Job() (or CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO), which adds a plain Job) is cancelled forever when any child fails with a non-cancellation exception. After that, every launch returns an already-cancelled job and runs nothing: no crash, no log, features "just stop" (periodic uploader stops uploading after one failed batch).

private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO)             // plain Job
scope.launch { upload(batch1) }        // throws -> scope is cancelled for good
scope.launch { upload(batch2) }        // silently never runs

Fixes.

  • Use SupervisorJob() for long-lived scopes with independent tasks.
  • Still catch per-task errors (supervisor does not stop the crash/handler).
  • Add a handler and retry/backoff in the loop (not in the handler).
  • Monitor scope.isActive in debug builds, or log in invokeOnCompletion of the scope's Job.

Real-life picture. A single blown fuse that switches off every light in the house because all lights share one fuse.

Common interview traps.

  • Using CoroutineScope(dispatcher) for a service scope.
  • Believing the scope recovers on its own.
  • Putting try/catch outside the while loop that launches the work.

notes.title: Exception routing in the Job tree
notes.html:
Path of a failure (JobSupport internals).

  1. A coroutine body throws; the coroutine's resumeWith(Result.failure(e)) runs and calls makeCompleting.
  2. The state moves to Cancelling with the cause (cancelParent(cause)). The coroutine first asks its parent: parentHandle.childCancelled(cause).
  3. A regular parent returns true ("handled") after cancelling itself, and the chain repeats upward until the root.
  4. A SupervisorJob (or a root without parent) returns false. Then this coroutine calls handleJobException(cause). For StandaloneCoroutine (launch) that calls handleCoroutineException(context, cause): it looks up the CoroutineExceptionHandler in the context; if absent, it calls the global handlers (ServiceLoader-registered, including the Android one) and Thread.currentThread().uncaughtExceptionHandler.
  5. DeferredCoroutine (async) does not call the handler; it stores the exception until await().
  6. CancellationException is excluded from steps 4 and from the parent's cancellation (childCancelled ignores it).
  7. After completion, exceptions are delivered to children first (cancellation goes down) before finally blocks complete.

Why a supervisor child "crashes the app". Supervisor childCancelled returned false -> step 4 -> no handler -> thread's uncaught handler -> process killed.

Real-life picture. A complaint goes up the management chain; the first manager with the authority "to deal with it" (a supervisor) receives it and files it; if no one handles it, it ends at the company's emergency line.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking handlers on any level are called.
  • Saying async calls the handler.
  • Not knowing childCancelled/handleJobException.

notes.title: Domain exceptions and layering
notes.html:
Idea. Each layer should expose errors in its own language. The data layer converts HttpException(404)/IOException/SQLiteException to domain errors (NotFound, Offline, PaymentDeclined), so the ViewModel and UI never depend on Retrofit or Room.

sealed class DomainError : Exception() { object Offline : DomainError(); data class Http(val code: Int) : DomainError() }
suspend fun load(): User = try { api.user() } catch (e: IOException) { throw DomainError.Offline }

Guidelines:

  • Wrap with the original as cause so Crashlytics keeps the root cause.
  • Don't convert CancellationException (let it flow).
  • Map at the boundary (repository), not in every call site.
  • Don't leak implementation exceptions across module APIs.

Industry examples. Clean Architecture in Swiggy/Paytm-like codebases (data, domain, presentation layers), Ktor's ClientRequestException mapped in a client layer.

Real-life picture. A hotel front desk translates "kitchen out of eggs" into "breakfast option unavailable" for guests.

Common interview traps.

  • Throwing HttpException into the UI.
  • Mapping everything to a generic Exception and losing the cause.
  • Converting cancellation into a domain error.

notes.title: Partial failure in fan-out
notes.html:
The decision. When you load several things in parallel (home screen: banner, feed, notifications), what should happen if one fails? Options:

Policy Tool Result
All-or-nothing coroutineScope { async... } first failure cancels others, whole load fails
Best-effort supervisorScope + per-task catch show what loaded; show per-section errors
Critical + optional critical in async, optional wrapped in runCatching-like catch (cancellation-safe) 
suspend fun loadHome(): Home = supervisorScope {
    val feed = async { runCatchingCancellable { api.feed() } }
    val ads  = async { runCatchingCancellable { api.ads() } }
    Home(feed.await(), ads.await())            // each is Result; UI handles sections
}

Silent swallowing in parallel loads (incident). A screen did launch { try { a() } catch (e: Exception) {} } for each section and showed an empty screen on failure with no error and no log; analytics showed "success" because the outer function returned normally. Fix: return per-section results with errors, log non-fatal exceptions, show retry per section.

Multi-bug review checklist. When reviewing coroutine code, scan for: try/catch around launch; catch (Exception) without rethrowing cancellation; launch(Job())/SupervisorJob() argument; handler on child; async without await; GlobalScope; runCatching in suspend code; plain Job() scope for long-lived work; retry inside handler; suspend calls in finally without NonCancellable; shared mutable state without synchronization; blocking calls on Main.

Real-life picture. A delivery of five parcels: if one is damaged you do not throw away the other four, you tell the customer which one is missing.

Common interview traps.

  • Using coroutineScope when partial results are acceptable.
  • Using supervisorScope and then never checking await failures.
  • Reporting "success" when sections silently failed.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• launch failures go up immediately; async failures are held until await() (but a child async also fails its parent).
  • try/catch around launch catches nothing; around coroutineScope/withContext/await it does.
  • Uncaught exceptions from root coroutines crash Android, even in viewModelScope (SupervisorJob only stops sideways cancellation).
  • CoroutineExceptionHandler works only on root coroutines, is for logging, ignores async, never sees cancellation and cannot retry.
  • CancellationException is not an error; an await on someone else's cancelled Deferred looks like your cancellation, so use ensureActive.
  • First exception wins, others are suppressed; handlers must never throw.
  • Catch narrow types; avoid runCatching and launchSafe that swallow cancellation.
  • A plain Job() scope dies on the first failure; use SupervisorJob and per-task catches.
  • Decide failure policy per operation (coroutineScope vs supervisorScope) and map exceptions to domain errors at the repository boundary.

questions.promptHtml: How does an exception thrown inside launch behave differently from one thrown inside async?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the entry question for exception handling. If you get it wrong, every later answer about handlers and supervisors falls apart.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: launch is fire-and-forget, so nobody is waiting to receive its exception. It propagates up the Job tree straight away. If it reaches the root unhandled, it goes to a CoroutineExceptionHandler or else to the thread's uncaught-exception handler, which on Android crashes the app. async returns a Deferred that can carry a result or an exception. As a root coroutine it stores the exception and rethrows it when someone calls await(). As a child it does both: it still cancels its parent right away, and await() also rethrows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each builder creates a coroutine that is also a Job. When the body throws, the coroutine moves to Cancelling and then Cancelled with that exception as the cause. After that, two separate questions decide what happens.

  1. Does the parent take responsibility? A child always reports a non-cancellation failure to its parent. A regular parent (Job, or a coroutine like launch) accepts it, cancels itself and its other children, and carries the exception upward. A supervisor parent refuses it.
  2. If nobody above takes it, who handles it? That depends on the builder. launch (StandaloneCoroutine) treats the exception as uncaught and hands it to handleCoroutineException. async (DeferredCoroutine) does not. It keeps the exception in its state for await() to rethrow.
                     launch                         async
child of a           cancels parent immediately     cancels parent immediately
regular parent       parent handles                 parent handles (await also rethrows)
root / child of      CEH or thread uncaught handler stored in Deferred
supervisor           -> crash on Android            -> rethrown on await(), silent if never awaited

The key point: async only "holds" the exception when nobody above it will accept it. Inside a regular hierarchy, the failure travels up immediately whether or not you ever call await().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)

scope.launch { throw IOException("from launch") }   // uncaught -> handler/thread -> crash on Android

val deferred = scope.async { throw IOException("from async") } // stored, nothing happens yet

scope.launch {
    try {
        deferred.await()                              // rethrown here
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        log("handled: ${e.message}")
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking async never crashes. Inside a launch, or inside coroutineScope, a failing async fails the parent even if await is wrapped in try/catch.
  • Thinking launch exceptions can be read from the returned Job. join() does not rethrow the failure.
  • Forgetting that an un-awaited root async loses its exception silently.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does await() throw if the Deferred was cancelled rather than failed? → A CancellationException. That can silently end the awaiting coroutine as well (see Q386).
  2. Does produce behave like launch or async? → Like async. The exception is exposed to the consumer through receive/iteration.
  3. Why didn't the library make launch store exceptions too? → Nobody would ever observe them. Silent loss is worse than a crash, so "uncaught" is the safe default.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people say "async throws on await, launch throws immediately." A senior separates the two questions (does the parent accept it, and if not, does the builder report it as uncaught) and uses that to predict every combination: child async, root async, async under a supervisor.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team replaced launch with async "to stop crashes" in a fire-and-forget analytics call. Crashes stopped. So did any visibility into failures, because the Deferred was never awaited.

questions.promptHtml: Why doesn't wrapping scope.launch { ... } in try/catch catch the exception thrown inside it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common junior bug in coroutine code. It checks whether you understand that launch returns before its body runs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: launch doesn't execute the body in my call stack. It schedules a new coroutine and returns a Job at once, so the try block has already exited by the time the body runs. The exception is then thrown on a different call stack, inside the dispatcher's task, and it propagates through the Job hierarchy, not through my stack frames. The try/catch has to go inside the coroutine, or around a suspending call that waits for the work, such as coroutineScope, withContext or await.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Exceptions travel along the call stack. launch creates a coroutine, gives it to the dispatcher (for Dispatchers.Main that's a Handler.post; for Default/IO it's a task in the scheduler queue), and returns. The thread that called launch leaves the try block. Later a worker thread runs DispatchedTask.run(), which resumes the coroutine. The body throws inside that frame. The coroutine machinery catches it, completes the Job exceptionally, and starts Job-tree propagation.

caller thread:   try { launch{...} } catch {...}   <- already finished
                        |
                        v (scheduled)
worker thread:   DispatchedTask.run -> body throws -> Job completes exceptionally
                                                  -> parent / handler / uncaught

Even CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED, which runs the body up to its first suspension in the caller's frame, doesn't help. The builder catches the exception internally and turns it into a Job failure. It never rethrows it to the caller.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: the catch never runs; with no handler the app crashes
fun refresh() {
    try {
        viewModelScope.launch { _items.value = repo.fetch() }
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        _error.value = e.message
    }
}

// Correct: catch where the work runs
fun refresh() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try {
            _items.value = repo.fetch()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            _error.value = e.message
        }
    }
}

// Also correct: a suspending boundary rethrows into the caller's coroutine
suspend fun loadBoth(): Pair<A, B> = try {
    coroutineScope { async { a() }.await() to async { b() }.await() }
} catch (e: IOException) {
    fallback()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting UNDISPATCHED or Dispatchers.Main.immediate to make the try/catch work. They don't.
  • Putting try/catch inside the coroutine but around a nested launch. Same bug, one level down.
  • Catching Exception inside the coroutine and swallowing CancellationException (cross-ref C5).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does try/catch around withContext work? → Yes. withContext suspends the caller and rethrows the block's exception into the caller's frame.
  2. Does try/catch around deferred.await() always prevent a crash? → No. If the async is a child of a regular parent, the parent is already failing (Q384).
  3. Can a CoroutineExceptionHandler replace the inner try/catch? → Only for logging and reporting. It runs after the coroutine is dead and can't recover or emit state (Q381).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "launch is async." The senior describes the actual mechanism (scheduled task, different stack, Job-tree propagation), and points out that suspending boundaries (coroutineScope, withContext, await) are where exceptions get back onto the caller's stack.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: This exact pattern turns up in code review all the time when callback code gets converted. The old try { api.enqueue(...) } habit carries over, and the first network timeout crashes the app.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly happens on Android when a coroutine throws and nothing handles the exception? Does it matter which dispatcher it ran on?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know the "uncaught" path ends in process death, and that moving work to Dispatchers.IO doesn't make it safe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The coroutine fails and propagates up. If no coroutine above it takes the exception and there's no CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, kotlinx.coroutines calls the current thread's uncaught-exception handler. On Android that's normally Crashlytics wrapping the platform's default handler, which kills the process. The dispatcher doesn't matter: an uncaught exception on an IO worker thread crashes the app the same way as one on main.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The path for an exception that reaches a root launch:

coroutine fails
  -> parent accepts? (regular Job parent, not supervisor) -> parent handles, repeat upward
  -> nobody accepts -> builder is launch/actor? (async keeps it) 
      -> handleCoroutineException(context, e)
           context[CoroutineExceptionHandler] != null -> call it, done
           else -> handleUncaughtCoroutineException:
                 1. ServiceLoader-registered handlers (kotlinx-coroutines-android
                    registers an Android pre-handler for platform logging)
                 2. Thread.currentThread().uncaughtExceptionHandler.uncaughtException(t, e)
                      -> Crashlytics / Sentry handler records it
                      -> delegates to Android's default handler -> process killed

Two Android-specific facts:

  • Any thread kills the process. Plain JVM servers often keep running when a worker thread dies. On Android, the default handler installed by the runtime kills the whole app, whether the thread is main, a DefaultDispatcher-worker, or your own executor.
  • Not like ExecutorService.submit. submit hides exceptions inside the Future. A coroutine launch deliberately does not. People coming from Executors expect silent failure and get crashes, which is the safer default.

Recent kotlinx.coroutines versions (the change landed in early 2022, PR #3170) also attach a suppressed DiagnosticCoroutineContextException to the exception before it reaches the thread handler. Its message is the coroutine's context, so the crash report shows which coroutine and dispatcher failed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncManager(private val api: Api) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) // no handler

    fun sync() {
        scope.launch { api.upload() } // SocketTimeoutException here = app crash, even on IO
    }
}

// Minimum safe version for fire-and-forget work
private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.w("Sync", "sync failed", e) }
private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking background threads "fail quietly" on Android.
  • Thinking viewModelScope or lifecycleScope catch exceptions. They install no handler, so an uncaught failure there crashes.
  • Using Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler to swallow exceptions globally. That leaves the app half-alive in a corrupt state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does an uncaught CancellationException crash the app? → No. Cancellation is treated as normal termination and never reaches handlers.
  2. Will Crashlytics show it as fatal or non-fatal? → Fatal, because it went through the uncaught handler. If you want a non-fatal record, log it yourself in a CEH or catch block.
  3. Can a CoroutineExceptionHandler prevent the crash? → Yes. When one is found in the context, the thread handler isn't called. But the coroutine is still dead and the state it was building is still unfinished.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "it crashes." The senior traces the full path (parent acceptance, builder type, handler lookup, ServiceLoader handlers, thread handler, process kill), knows the dispatcher is irrelevant, and contrasts this with Executor.submit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "background sync" moved to CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) was assumed to be safe from crashes. It became the top Crashlytics fatal the week it shipped, driven by UnknownHostException on flaky networks.

questions.promptHtml: What is a CoroutineExceptionHandler, what is it good for, and what can it not do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates treat CEH as a coroutine try/catch. Interviewers want to hear that it's a last-resort reporter, not a recovery mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CEH is a context element that's called only for uncaught exceptions, meaning exceptions no parent took and no await consumed. By the time it runs, the coroutine has already completed with that exception, so I can't resume, retry in place, or return a value. I use it for logging, crash reporting, and maybe a generic UI signal. Recovery belongs in try/catch inside the coroutine, or in Result types.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Shape: CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, throwable -> ... } is a CoroutineContext.Element with key CoroutineExceptionHandler. You add it with + like any other element.
  • When it runs: after the failing coroutine and all its children have finished. The parent waits for its children to terminate before handling the original exception. It runs on whatever thread completed the coroutine. Don't assume main.
  • What it never sees:
    • CancellationException (normal cancellation),
    • exceptions from async (they belong to the Deferred),
    • exceptions from children whose parent takes the failure (Q383 covers placement),
    • exceptions rethrown to a caller by coroutineScope/withContext/runBlocking.
  • What it can't do: prevent sibling cancellation in a regular hierarchy, keep the coroutine alive, or return a fallback value.
Need Tool
Recover and show an error state try/catch inside the coroutine, or a Result type
Keep siblings alive when one fails SupervisorJob / supervisorScope
Log/report anything that slipped through CoroutineExceptionHandler
Combine results that may fail async + await in try/catch, inside supervisorScope

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val reportingHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, e ->
    // Runs on the completing thread; post to main if you touch UI state.
    crashReporter.recordNonFatal(e, context[CoroutineName]?.name)
}

fun prefetch() {
    viewModelScope.launch(reportingHandler + CoroutineName("prefetch")) {
        cache.warm(api.popular())   // failure: logged as non-fatal, no crash, no UI change
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Updating UI state from the handler without thinking about threads, or treating it as the main error-UI path. You end up with a generic "Something went wrong" that has no context.
  • Calling launch again from inside the handler for "retry" with no limit. That gives you an infinite retry loop with no backoff.
  • Expecting it to fire for async.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the handler itself throws? → The library wraps both exceptions and sends them to the thread's uncaught handler, so you crash anyway (Q395).
  2. Is CEH inherited by children? → The element is inherited like any other context element, but it's only consulted at the coroutine that ends up handling the exception.
  3. Can you install a global one? → Not through a public API. There is a ServiceLoader-based hook (CoroutineExceptionHandler service in META-INF/services) that the library calls for uncaught exceptions, but it doesn't stop the crash. Treat it as an advanced, rarely justified hook.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE it's "a catch block for coroutines." The senior says "last-resort reporter, runs after death, never for cancellation or async," and gives a decision table for what to use instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put _uiState.value = Error in a shared CEH. Since the handler couldn't tell a failed prefetch from a failed checkout, a background prefetch failure wiped out a working screen with an error page.

questions.promptHtml: If I start several children inside coroutineScope { } and one fails, what happens, and where can I catch it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: coroutineScope is the standard way to do parallel decomposition inside a suspend function. The interviewer is checking that you know the failure comes back to the caller as an ordinary exception.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: coroutineScope is a regular, non-supervisor scope. If any child fails, it cancels its remaining children, waits for them to finish, and then rethrows the original exception from the coroutineScope call itself. It doesn't go to a handler. So the try/catch goes around coroutineScope, not around individual awaits inside it. withContext behaves the same way for its block.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
coroutineScope and withContext create a scoped coroutine. Internally it's marked as scoped, so a failing child doesn't push the failure further up the Job tree. Instead it is thrown back to the suspended caller. The order of events:

coroutineScope {
   a = async { ... }   b = async { throw IOException }   c = launch { ... }
}
1. b fails -> notifies scope (regular parent accepts)
2. scope enters Cancelling -> cancels a and c (they get CancellationException at next suspension)
3. scope waits for a and c to finish (their finally blocks run)
4. coroutineScope(...) call throws IOException in the caller

Effects:

  • Fail-fast. One failed child stops the whole decomposition. That's usually what you want: no half-loaded dashboard built on bad assumptions.
  • No partial results unless you switch to supervisorScope and handle each child's result yourself.
  • Exception identity. The caller gets the original exception type (IOException), so catch (e: IOException) works. Other children's failures may be attached as suppressed (Q387).
  • The body counts too. If the block itself throws after starting children, the same thing happens: children are cancelled and awaited, then the exception is rethrown.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadProfile(id: String): Profile = coroutineScope {
    val user = async { api.user(id) }
    val posts = async { api.posts(id) }
    Profile(user.await(), posts.await())
}

// Caller decides the policy in one place
viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.value = try {
        UiState.Content(loadProfile(id))
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        UiState.Error(e)
    }
}

// Broken: catching around one await does not save the scope
suspend fun broken() = coroutineScope {
    val a = async { throw IOException() }
    val b = async { api.b() }
    val safeA = try { a.await() } catch (e: IOException) { null } // caught...
    safeA to b.await() // ...but the scope is already cancelled; coroutineScope still throws IOException
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Catching inside the scope around await and assuming the failure is contained.
  • Expecting a CoroutineExceptionHandler on the outer launch to receive the exception when the caller has already caught it. It won't; a caught exception isn't uncaught.
  • Using supervisorScope "to be safe" and then never checking the individual children, which turns failures into silent gaps.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does withContext differ? → It runs one block, possibly on another dispatcher. Its failure and its children's failures are rethrown the same way.
  2. Does coroutineScope return before its launch children finish? → No. It waits for all children to complete, success or failure.
  3. Where does a failure of runBlocking's children go? → runBlocking also rethrows to its caller. That's why tests using it see the exception directly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people know "one fails, all fail." The senior explains the cancel-then-wait-then-rethrow sequence, that the original exception type reaches the caller (so typed catch works), and that the policy decision belongs at the call site.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen loaded price, stock and shipping in a coroutineScope. A shipping-API outage made every checkout fail. The fix was a business decision: keep price and stock fail-fast, and move shipping into its own supervised, defaulted branch.

questions.promptHtml: Where does a CoroutineExceptionHandler have to be installed to actually be invoked? Why is a handler on a child coroutine ignored?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "My handler isn't called" is one of the most common coroutine bugs. A good answer explains the rule mechanically instead of reciting "only at the root."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A handler is consulted only by the coroutine that ends up being responsible for the exception: the one whose parent refuses it. In practice that's a coroutine launched directly in a scope (the scope's Job takes no responsibility), a coroutine directly under a SupervisorJob or supervisorScope, or a true root launched with no parent. A handler on a nested launch under a regular parent is ignored because the parent accepts the failure. A handler on async is always ignored, because async puts its exception in the Deferred.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When a coroutine finishes with a non-cancellation exception, its job runs roughly this:

handled = notifyParent(e)            // parent.childCancelled(e)
          || handleJobException(e)   // launch: call CEH or thread handler; async: no-op

What childCancelled returns depends on the parent:

Parent Accepts the child's failure? Who looks up the CEH
Another coroutine (launch, async, coroutineScope...) Yes The parent (recursively)
SupervisorJob() / supervisorScope No The child itself
Plain Job() that is the scope's root (e.g. CoroutineScope(Job())) Cancels itself, but reports "not handled" because it has no handling parent The child itself
No parent (GlobalScope) No The child itself

So "root" really means "the topmost coroutine in the chain that has to handle it." With CoroutineScope(Job() + handler).launch { throw }, the handler is invoked and the scope's Job is cancelled. The scope then can't start new coroutines, which is a separate trap (see Q397).

The handler is looked up in that coroutine's own context, which includes elements inherited from the scope. That's why putting the handler in the scope's context works: every top-level launch inherits it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val scopeHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log("scope handler: $e") }
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + scopeHandler)

scope.launch {                                        // responsible coroutine -> uses scopeHandler
    launch(CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, _ ->
        log("child handler")                          // NEVER called: parent accepts
    }) {
        throw IOException("boom")
    }
}

scope.async(CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, _ ->
    log("async handler")                              // NEVER called: async stores it
}) { throw IOException("boom") }

scope.launch {
    supervisorScope {
        launch(CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
            log("supervised child handler: $e")       // CALLED: supervisor refuses responsibility
        }) { throw IOException("boom") }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing the handler to withContext(handler) { launch { throw } }. The launch is a child of withContext's scoped coroutine, which accepts the failure and rethrows it to the caller. The handler isn't used.
  • Thinking the handler on the scope.launch call is "more specific" than the one in the scope. It is: the coroutine's context has the closest one, and that one wins. People mix this up with nested launches, where the inner handler is ignored.
  • Assuming runBlocking(handler) catches children's failures. runBlocking rethrows to the caller.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. With a plain Job() scope plus a handler, what is the observable difference from SupervisorJob()? → The handler fires in both cases. With Job() the scope is also cancelled, so siblings die and later launch calls do nothing.
  2. Why did the library designers make child handlers ignored? → The parent is going to fail anyway with the same exception. Handling it at the child as well would report it twice and suggest the failure was contained when it wasn't.
  3. Can lifecycleScope.launch(handler) prevent a crash? → Yes, that launch is directly under the scope's SupervisorJob, so its handler is used.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "install it on the root." The senior gives the responsibility rule (who refuses, who handles), shows the Job() vs SupervisorJob() difference, and lists the scoped-builder exceptions (withContext, coroutineScope, runBlocking).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team had a 40-line "error handler" attached to every nested launch inside a single parent launch, and none of them ever ran. Crashes were being reported only through the global handler, and that was mistaken for "the handler is broken."

questions.promptHtml: Compare a root async with a child async. When does each one's exception surface, and can it ever be lost silently?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can reason about the hierarchy rather than the builder name. The viewModelScope.async case catches out even experienced developers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A child async under a regular parent fails the parent immediately, whether or not anyone awaits it, and await() also rethrows. A root async holds the exception in its Deferred and rethrows only on await(). Here's the subtle part: async launched directly in a SupervisorJob scope such as viewModelScope acts like a root. The supervisor refuses the failure and async doesn't report it as uncaught, so if nobody awaits it, the exception disappears without a log.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Case                                         On failure                       If never awaited
GlobalScope.async {}                         stored                           LOST silently
viewModelScope.async {}  (SupervisorJob)     stored                           LOST silently
CoroutineScope(Job()).async {}               scope Job cancelled + stored     scope dead, exception never seen
launch { async {} }                          parent launch fails at once      parent fails -> handler/crash
coroutineScope { async {} }                  scope fails, rethrows to caller  rethrown anyway
supervisorScope { async {} }                 stored                           LOST silently

Why the silent loss: two rules combine. The supervisor says "not my problem," and DeferredCoroutine says "I don't report uncaught, the awaiter will." If no awaiter ever comes, nobody hears about it.

Why the child-async surprise: inside launch { val d = async { fail() }; try { d.await() } catch(...) {} }, the async notifies its parent launch when it fails, not when you await. The parent goes into Cancelling. Your catch around await does catch the rethrown exception, but the parent is already failing and will crash the app or fail the scope once its body finishes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Silent loss: no crash, no log, nothing
fun preload() {
    viewModelScope.async { api.prefetch() }   // Deferred dropped
}

// Surprise crash: try/catch around await doesn't save the parent
fun load() = viewModelScope.launch {
    val d = async { api.data() }              // child of launch
    val data = try { d.await() } catch (e: IOException) { null }
    show(data)                                // never reached; launch is cancelled, then crashes
}

// Correct: either handle inside the async, or isolate with supervisorScope
fun loadFixed() = viewModelScope.launch {
    val data = supervisorScope {
        val d = async { api.data() }
        try { d.await() } catch (e: IOException) { null }
    }
    show(data)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using async without await as a "launch that doesn't crash." That's silent failure by design.
  • Assuming the try around await in the child case means the error is handled.
  • Lint won't save you. DeferredResultUnused-style inspections catch some unused Deferreds, but not one stored in a field and never awaited.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. In loadFixed, why doesn't the supervisorScope fail? → Its child async failed, but supervisors don't take child failures. Only the body's own exceptions fail it, and the body caught the await.
  2. Is async { }.await() immediately afterwards ever useful? → No. Use withContext or call the function directly. It adds a coroutine and nothing else.
  3. How would you find silently lost Deferreds in a large codebase? → Search for async { whose result isn't awaited, plus a detekt/lint rule. At runtime, DebugProbes can dump coroutines in a completed/failed state (C32 owns the tooling).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "async throws on await." The senior builds the full matrix, gives the viewModelScope.async silent-loss case, and explains the child case where the parent is already doomed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "parallel prefetch" written as viewModelScope.async in an init block failed on 100% of devices after a backend contract change, and for three weeks nobody knew. The only symptom was a slower first screen, because the cache was always empty.

questions.promptHtml: How do exceptions behave inside supervisorScope? Which handler is used, and what happens if the supervisorScope body itself throws?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: People pick supervisorScope to "make errors not crash." It doesn't do that, and the interviewer wants to hear what it actually changes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: supervisorScope changes one thing: a failing child no longer cancels the scope or its siblings. Each direct child is responsible for its own exception. A child launch looks up a CoroutineExceptionHandler in its own context, which includes whatever the outer coroutine had, and with no handler it goes to the thread's uncaught handler, which still crashes. A child async keeps its exception for await. If the supervisorScope body throws, the scope fails like a normal scope: it cancels all children and rethrows to the caller.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Failures only flow downward. A child failure stops at the supervisor. Cancelling the supervisor (or the body failing) still cancels every child.
  • Direct children only. Grandchildren live under a regular child launch, so a grandchild failure cancels that child, and the child then reports to the supervisor. Supervision doesn't extend down the tree.
  • Handler lookup. supervisorScope inherits the caller's context. If the outer launch was started with a handler, the children see it and use it. In viewModelScope there's no handler by default, so supervised children crash the app just as before.
  • Completion. supervisorScope waits for all children. It returns normally even if every child failed, as long as the body didn't throw.
supervisorScope {             failure of child A:
   A = launch {...}             A -> CEH in A's context, or thread handler (crash)
   B = async  {...}           B stored in Deferred
   C = launch { launch {X} }  X fails -> cancels C (regular parent) -> C -> CEH/crash
   throw IllegalState()       body throws -> cancels A, B, C, waits, rethrows to caller
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private val logOnly = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Log.w(TAG, "widget failed", e) }

fun refreshWidgets() = viewModelScope.launch(logOnly) {
    supervisorScope {
        widgets.forEach { w ->
            launch {                      // inherits logOnly; one failure doesn't stop the others
                _widgetState.update { it + (w.id to w.load()) }
            }
        }
    }
    _refreshing.value = false            // reached even if some widgets failed
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• launch(SupervisorJob()) { ... } "to supervise." That replaces the parent link, so the coroutine is no longer a child of the scope and outlives cancellation (C4 owns this bug).
  • Expecting supervision for grandchildren.
  • Using supervisorScope without a handler or inner try/catch, so failures still crash, only one at a time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. supervisorScope vs a scope built on SupervisorJob()? → Same child semantics. supervisorScope is a suspending call that waits for its children and rethrows body failures. A SupervisorJob scope is a long-lived container you own and must cancel.
  2. If every child fails, does the caller know? → Not unless you collect results. Use async plus per-child try/catch around await, or have children write into a Result list.
  3. Does withContext(SupervisorJob()) give you supervision? → No, and it breaks structured concurrency. The new Job becomes the parent of the block, and the caller's cancellation no longer flows into it. Use supervisorScope.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "supervisorScope makes children independent." The senior adds: direct children only, uncaught still crashes without a handler, the body failure still cancels everything, and an explicit per-child result is needed if the caller has to know about partial failure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed with 8 independent carousels used supervisorScope without a handler. One carousel's backend started returning malformed JSON and crashed 2% of sessions. "Independent" turned out not to mean "safe."

questions.promptHtml: Why are CancellationExceptions ignored by exception handlers and not propagated to the parent as a failure? How can that bite you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The special treatment of CancellationException explains several "my coroutine just stopped, no crash, no log" incidents. Seniors are expected to know the dangerous cases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The machinery treats CancellationException as normal termination, not as an error. A child that ends with it doesn't cancel its parent, and no CoroutineExceptionHandler or uncaught handler is ever called. That's what allows job.cancel() to work without crashing anything. The problem: any CancellationException gets this treatment, including one you didn't intend. A business exception that extends it, a TimeoutCancellationException escaping an inner withTimeout, or await() on a Deferred that was cancelled will all end your coroutine silently.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The check is by type. When a coroutine completes with an exception e:

  • if e is CancellationException, parent notification returns "handled" without cancelling the parent, and the handler path is skipped;
  • otherwise the parent is cancelled, or the handler/uncaught path runs.

On the JVM, kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException is a typealias for java.util.concurrent.CancellationException, which extends IllegalStateException. So the type check also covers anything you create with those classes.

Ways an unintended cancellation exception ends a coroutine silently:

Source Why it's cancellation-typed
class UserAbortException : CancellationException() Explicit subclass, often written to make a coroutine "stop cleanly"
withTimeout inside a launch that isn't itself timed out TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException subclass, so the launch ends quietly (timeout details are in C5)
deferred.await() where the deferred was cancelled by someone else await rethrows the deferred's CancellationException into the awaiting coroutine
channel.receive() on a cancelled channel Throws CancellationException
java.util.concurrent.CancellationException from a Future/Guava interop Same JVM type

Only the coroutine that is actually being cancelled should stop. In the await case the awaiter isn't being cancelled; it just received a cancellation-typed exception. Since kotlinx.coroutines treats them the same, the awaiter completes as "cancelled" and nothing reports it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bug: polling silently dies the first time a request takes > 5s
fun startPolling() = viewModelScope.launch {
    while (true) {
        val status = withTimeout(5_000) { api.status() }  // TimeoutCancellationException escapes
        _status.value = status
        delay(10_000)
    }
}

// Fix: make the timeout an explicit, non-cancellation outcome
fun startPolling() = viewModelScope.launch {
    while (true) {
        val status = withTimeoutOrNull(5_000) { api.status() }
        if (status != null) _status.value = status else _status.value = Status.Stale
        delay(10_000)
    }
}

// Defensive await of something another component may cancel
suspend fun <T> Deferred<T>.awaitOrFailure(): T {
    try {
        return await()
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()           // if WE are cancelled, rethrow normally
        throw IllegalStateException("Upstream deferred was cancelled", e) // otherwise it's a real failure
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Defining domain exceptions that extend CancellationException "so they don't crash."
  • Catching CancellationException and not rethrowing it when your own coroutine really is being cancelled (cross-ref C5).
  • Assuming a coroutine that "stopped working" must have crashed. Check invokeOnCompletion causes instead (Q389).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. If a child throws CancellationException, does the parent continue? → Yes. Only that child ends; parent and siblings carry on.
  2. job.cancel(CancellationException("reason", cause)): does the cause reach handlers? → No handler is called for cancellation. The cause is visible through invokeOnCompletion or a catch in the coroutine.
  3. How would you detect silent cancellations in production? → invokeOnCompletion { cause -> if (cause is CancellationException && !intentionalStop) log(cause) } on long-lived jobs, plus coroutine names in the logs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "cancellation isn't an error, so don't swallow it." The senior knows the type-based rule and lists the unintended sources (timeouts, cancelled Deferreds, Java CancellationException interop, custom subclasses), with a defensive pattern for each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A live-score screen stopped updating for a subset of users with no crash and no log. The cause was an inner withTimeout(3_000) on a slow endpoint during peak traffic, which silently ended the polling loop.

questions.promptHtml: If several children of the same parent fail at almost the same time, which exception does the handler or caller receive, and what happens to the others?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a detail that matters when you read crash reports from parallel code. Seniors are expected to know that later failures aren't lost and where to look for them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The first exception wins. The parent completes with the first non-cancellation exception it was notified of. Exceptions that arrive later while the parent is already cancelling, from other children or from children's finally blocks, are attached as suppressed exceptions on the first one through Throwable.addSuppressed. CancellationExceptions caused by the cascade aren't added. On the JVM you see them as Suppressed: entries in the stack trace. The kotlinlang docs say aggregation works on Java 1.7+ and is limited on JS/Native.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
While a Job is Cancelling, it collects the exceptions that its children and its own body complete with. When it finishes, it picks the root cause:

  1. the first non-cancellation exception, if any;
  2. otherwise a CancellationException (so the whole thing was just cancelled).

It then adds the other distinct non-cancellation exceptions to the root cause as suppressed. The same exception instance isn't added twice, and cancellation exceptions are skipped. Stack-trace recovery copies (debug mode) are unwrapped so that the same failure doesn't appear twice.

parent
 ├─ child A throws IOException            (t=0ms)   -> root cause
 ├─ child B, on cancel, finally throws     (t=2ms)   -> suppressed on IOException
 │   IllegalStateException("close failed")
 └─ child C cancelled normally             (t=3ms)   -> ignored (CancellationException)

Crash report:
java.io.IOException: connection reset
    at ...
    Suppressed: java.lang.IllegalStateException: close failed

Separately, when an exception reaches the thread's uncaught handler, newer library versions add a DiagnosticCoroutineContextException (introduced in 2022 via PR #3170) as one more suppressed entry. Its message is the coroutine context, for example [CoroutineName(sync), StandaloneCoroutine{Cancelling}@..., Dispatchers.IO]. Don't mistake it for a second failure.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
    log("root=${e::class.simpleName} suppressed=${e.suppressed.map { it::class.simpleName }}")
}

CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + handler).launch {
    launch {
        try { awaitCancellation() } finally { throw IllegalStateException("cleanup failed") }
    }
    launch {
        delay(10)
        throw IOException("network")
    }
}
// root=IOException suppressed=[IllegalStateException]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the visible top exception when the suppressed one is the real bug (for example, a cleanup that throws and hides a resource leak).
  • Crash grouping in Crashlytics is driven by the top exception, so suppressed failures never get their own issue. They're easy to miss.
  • Assuming "first" means "first child in source order." It means first to arrive, so the reported type can vary between runs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does awaitAll aggregate? → awaitAll fails with the first failed Deferred's exception. Under a regular parent, the parent then aggregates as above.
  2. What if the root cause is a CancellationException but a child later failed for real? → A real failure during cancellation does propagate. Cancellation doesn't hide a genuine exception from a child; the failure is reported.
  3. Can I see every child failure in a supervisor? → Yes, because each child handles its own, so each appears separately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people say "the first exception." The senior explains the Cancelling-state collection, why cancellations are skipped, where Suppressed: appears, the diagnostic context entry, and why crash grouping hides secondary failures.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team spent a week on IOException crashes, and the real defect was a suppressed SQLiteException from a finally that wrote to a closed database. It only appeared under the top exception.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate adds error handling to a ViewModel after Crashlytics shows HttpException: HTTP 503 as the #2 fatal (0.6% of sessions, ~1.2M DAU). The PR description says "added CoroutineExceptionHandler, crash fixed." QA can't reproduce because staging never returns 503. The code:

class OrdersViewModel(private val repo: OrdersRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
        _state.value = OrdersState.Error(e.message ?: "unknown")
    }
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<OrdersState>(OrdersState.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<OrdersState> = _state

    fun load() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val orders = async(handler) { repo.orders() }
            val badges = async(handler) { repo.badges() }
            launch(handler) { repo.markSeen() }
            _state.value = OrdersState.Content(orders.await(), badges.await())
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Does this fix the crash? Walk me through what happens on a 503 from repo.orders(), and rewrite it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, the handler catches it and shows an error." Or "Move the handler to the async." The first is wrong; the second doesn't understand the rule. Both fail because they treat CEH as a local catch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Should a failed badges() blank out the whole screen, or should orders still show? That decides supervisor vs fail-fast.
    • Is markSeen() best effort? If it is, it must never affect UI state.
    • Is _state read anywhere off main? The handler would run on the completing thread.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Don't merge this as a "fix." If it's already shipped, the crash rate won't move, so I'd hotfix with a try/catch inside the parent launch. That's the smallest change that stops the crash.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what actually happens on a 503):
    • orders async is a child of the outer launch, so its handler is ignored, because async never uses handlers and its parent accepts the failure anyway.
    • The failure cancels the outer launch, which cancels badges and markSeen.
    • The outer launch is directly under viewModelScope's SupervisorJob, so it has to handle the exception itself. It looks in its own context and finds no handler, because the handler was passed to the children, not to it.
    • Result: thread uncaught handler, so the crash persists. orders.await() would also rethrow, but the parent is already cancelling.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with runTest, a fake repo that throws HttpException, and Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher()). With no handler on the parent, runTest reports the uncaught exception and fails the test, which is exactly the signal I want. A log line in the handler would show it never fires.
  5. Root cause: The handler is attached where it's never consulted. And even if it had been on the parent, writing UI state from a handler runs after the coroutine died. That's acceptable for a fallback, but it's the wrong main path.
  6. Fix:
fun load() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = try {
            coroutineScope {
                val orders = async { repo.orders() }
                val badges = async { runCatchingNonCancellation { repo.badges() }.getOrDefault(emptyList()) }
                OrdersState.Content(orders.await(), badges.await())
            }
        } catch (e: HttpException) {
            OrdersState.Error(e.code().toString())
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            OrdersState.Error("offline")
        }
    }
    viewModelScope.launch(reportOnlyHandler) { repo.markSeen() } // best effort, isolated
}

// Rethrows cancellation, wraps everything else
suspend inline fun <T> runCatchingNonCancellation(block: () -> T): Result<T> =
    try { Result.success(block()) } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { Result.failure(e) }

Badges failure now degrades gracefully; an orders failure gives an error state; markSeen can never break the screen. 7. Prevention: A detekt custom rule or review checklist item: "CEH passed to async or to a nested launch = bug." A unit test per ViewModel load path with a throwing fake. A Crashlytics alert on HttpException fatals. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't put a handler on viewModelScope via a custom scope that turns every failure into Error. That's the same coupling problem as the original. I also wouldn't catch Throwable, which swallows real bugs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if they move handler to the outer launch(handler)? → No crash, but the screen goes to Error on a badges failure too, and the handler writes state off the expected path. It's better, but still wrong for the product requirement.
  • What about supervisorScope instead of coroutineScope? → Then an orders failure is caught at orders.await() only if I put try/catch around it. Fine, but for "orders must succeed" fail-fast is the simpler model.
  • Why inline on the helper? → So the block can call suspend functions without being a suspend lambda. It's a convenience, not a requirement.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: I've seen a "crash fixed" PR like this ship and the crash curve not move at all. The reviewer had pattern-matched on "has a CoroutineExceptionHandler." Since then my review checklist asks where the handler sits, not whether one exists.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes the handler catches it; can't explain why async ignores handlers.
  • Hire: identifies parent-handles rule and the missing root handler; fixes with try/catch inside the launch.
  • Strong hire: also asks the product question (partial vs fail-fast), isolates best-effort work, keeps cancellation intact in the helper, and adds a test that proves the crash is gone.

questions.promptHtml: I have a Job from launch and a Deferred from async. How do I find out from outside whether each one failed, was cancelled, or succeeded?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Long-lived jobs (sync, polling, uploads) need monitoring, and many developers assume join() throws on failure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a Deferred, await() returns the value or rethrows the failure. For a Job, join() does not rethrow the job's failure; it only waits, and it throws only if the coroutine calling join is itself cancelled. To tell outcomes apart I use invokeOnCompletion { cause -> }: null means success, a CancellationException means it was cancelled, anything else means it failed. Properties like isCancelled are true for both failed and cancelled, so they can't separate the two.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Signal Success Cancelled Failed
isCompleted true true true
isCancelled false true true
join() returns returns returns (but if the job is your child, you get cancelled, so join throws CancellationException)
await() value throws CancellationException throws the exception
invokeOnCompletion(cause) null CancellationException the exception

Notes:

  • invokeOnCompletion handlers run synchronously in whatever thread completes the job. Keep them small, non-blocking and thread-safe. If one throws, the library wraps it in CompletionHandlerException and sends it to the exception handler path, not back to you.
  • If you register after completion, the handler is called immediately.
  • Deferred.getCompletionExceptionOrNull() exists but is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. Job.getCancellationException() is marked internal. Prefer invokeOnCompletion.
  • join on a child that failed: the failure has already cancelled you (the parent), so join throws CancellationException. This is the "join threw and I don't know why" trap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Uploader(private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    fun start(file: File): Job =
        scope.launch(CoroutineName("upload-${file.name}")) { api.upload(file) }
            .also { job ->
                job.invokeOnCompletion { cause ->
                    when (cause) {
                        null -> metrics.count("upload_ok")
                        is CancellationException -> metrics.count("upload_cancelled")
                        else -> metrics.count("upload_failed", cause::class.simpleName)
                    }
                }
            }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• job.join(); if (!job.isCancelled) showSuccess(). That's correct only because isCancelled covers failure. People then read "isCancelled" as "user cancelled," which is wrong.
  • Doing heavy work or touching UI inside invokeOnCompletion.
  • Using invokeOnCompletion as the error handler without a CEH. If the launch is at the root, it still crashes the app; invokeOnCompletion only observes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is invokeOnCompletion called before or after children finish? → After the job and all its children are complete. There's also an internal "on cancelling" variant, not public API for this purpose.
  2. How do I expose upload outcomes to the UI? → Don't rely on Job state. Model it as a StateFlow<UploadState> that the coroutine updates in try/catch/finally.
  3. Can the handler leak memory? → Yes. It holds references until the job completes. For long-running jobs, capture only what you need and use the returned DisposableHandle to unregister early.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "await throws, join doesn't." The senior gives the full outcome table, the child-join cancellation trap, the threading and exception rules of completion handlers, and prefers explicit state over reading Job flags.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upload queue reported "100% success" because it checked join() returning. Failed uploads looked identical, and roughly 3% of photos were silently never synced.

questions.subtopic: What to catch: Exception vs Throwable vs specific types
questions.promptHtml: Inside coroutines, should I catch Throwable, Exception, or specific types like IOException? What changes compared with normal Kotlin code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Catch-all blocks are where coroutine bugs hide. This checks that you know the JVM type hierarchy around CancellationException and what you can and can't recover from.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I catch the specific, expected types: IOException for network, HttpException for HTTP errors, my own domain exceptions. In coroutines a broad catch (e: Exception) also catches CancellationException, because on the JVM it extends IllegalStateException. So any broad catch has to rethrow cancellation first. I almost never catch Throwable mid-stack, since that swallows OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError and initialization errors that the process can't recover from. Only top-level reporting boundaries see everything, and they report and rethrow.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Throwable
 ├─ Error                      OOM, StackOverflowError, ExceptionInInitializerError, NoClassDefFoundError
 └─ Exception
     ├─ IOException            SocketTimeoutException, UnknownHostException, SSLException
     ├─ RuntimeException
     │   ├─ IllegalStateException
     │   │   └─ java.util.concurrent.CancellationException  == kotlin...CancellationException (JVM)
