     │   │        └─ TimeoutCancellationException, JobCancellationException (internal)
     │   └─ HttpException (Retrofit), SQLiteException, SerializationException ...
     └─ ...

Consequences:

  • catch (e: IllegalStateException), written to handle a check() failure, also catches cancellation. Yes, even that narrow-looking catch.
  • catch (e: Exception) around a suspend call turns cancellation into "an error." The coroutine then carries on past a point where it should have stopped, which can mean writing state for a screen that's gone.
  • catch (e: Throwable) also hides programmer bugs like NullPointerException (a RuntimeException) and fatal errors. A coroutine that hits OOM and carries on usually fails worse a moment later.
  • Expected vs unexpected: network, IO, HTTP 4xx/5xx and parsing failures from the server are expected, so map them to state. NPE, ClassCastException, IllegalArgumentException from your own code are bugs, so let them crash or report them as fatal. Catching them hides regressions from your crash-free metric.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Recommended shape at a repository/use-case boundary
suspend fun fetchOrders(): OrdersResult = try {
    OrdersResult.Success(api.orders())
} catch (e: IOException) {
    OrdersResult.Offline
} catch (e: HttpException) {
    if (e.code() == 401) OrdersResult.Unauthorized else OrdersResult.ServerError(e.code())
} catch (e: SerializationException) {
    reporter.nonFatal(e)                     // server contract broke; expected-ish, but worth alerting
    OrdersResult.ServerError(-1)
}

// If you truly need a broad catch
try {
    work()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: Exception) {
    reporter.nonFatal(e)
    fallback()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• runCatching { suspendCall() }, which catches Throwable, cancellation included (cross-ref C5 for the cancellation side).
  • Catching Exception in Room/DB code and continuing after an SQLiteFullException, which loses data silently.
  • Order of catch clauses: putting catch (e: Exception) before catch (e: CancellationException) means the second clause never runs. Catch clauses are checked top to bottom, so the narrow type has to come first.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException an IOException? → No, it's an IllegalArgumentException subclass, so it needs its own clause.
  2. What about OkHttp InterruptedIOException after cancellation? → It can come up when a call is cancelled. Check ensureActive() before mapping it to "offline" (C5 covers OkHttp cancellation).
  3. Should a catch (e: Throwable) ever exist? → At process-level boundaries (a worker's top level, a reporting wrapper) that log and rethrow, or that return Result.failure() to WorkManager while rethrowing cancellation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "catch Exception and show an error." The senior draws the hierarchy, explains why even an IllegalStateException catch catches cancellation, separates expected from programmer errors, and keeps bugs visible in crash metrics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A blanket catch (e: Exception) { showRetry() } in a base ViewModel held the crash-free rate at 99.95% while an NPE regression broke checkout for 4% of users. It only came to light through a conversion-rate dashboard.

questions.promptHtml: What are the options for handling errors from coroutines in a ViewModel, and which do you use by default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every Android codebase has to choose here. The interviewer wants a reasoned default, not "it depends."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: viewModelScope is SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate with no exception handler. So a failing launch doesn't affect its sibling launches, but an uncaught failure crashes the app. My default: repositories and use cases throw only for unexpected bugs and return typed results for expected failures. The ViewModel maps those results to UI state inside the launch, and a small report-only CoroutineExceptionHandler on fire-and-forget launches records anything unexpected as non-fatal. I don't use one global catch-all that turns every failure into a generic error screen.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy Pros Cons Use when
try/catch inside each launch, mapping to UiState.Error Explicit, local, testable Repetition, easy to forget, easy to over-catch Screen-critical loads, user actions
Repository returns Result/sealed outcome Errors are part of the type, so the compiler forces you to handle them More types; risk of wrapping bugs as "failures" Expected failures: offline, 4xx, validation
Report-only CEH on specific launches Nothing slips out to a crash for best-effort work Can't produce state; runs after death Prefetch, analytics, markSeen
A launchSafe(onError) extension Less repetition Hides the policy; tends to grow into a catch-all Only if it rethrows cancellation and narrows the types
Custom scope viewModelScope + handler everywhere Everything is caught Bugs become silent error screens; crash metrics lie Almost never

Points that matter:

  • Main.immediate. State updates in the catch block run on main without a re-dispatch when you're already on main, so _state.value = Error is safe there.
  • Errors as state, not events. Store the error in UiState (with retry info) so it survives configuration changes. One-off event delivery is covered in F2b.
  • Retry. The UI calls retry(), which starts a new launch. Don't retry from inside a handler (Q399).
  • Loading/finally. Clear isLoading in finally, so it's reset on success, failure and cancellation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileViewModel(private val getProfile: GetProfileUseCase) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProfileUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<ProfileUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    private val reportOnly = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Reporter.nonFatal(e) }

    fun load(id: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(loading = true, error = null) }
            try {
                when (val r = getProfile(id)) {          // returns a sealed outcome
                    is ProfileResult.Ok -> _state.update { it.copy(profile = r.profile) }
                    ProfileResult.Offline -> _state.update { it.copy(error = UiError.Offline) }
                    is ProfileResult.NotFound -> _state.update { it.copy(error = UiError.NotFound) }
                }
            } finally {
                _state.update { it.copy(loading = false) }
            }
        }
    }

    fun prefetchAvatars() {
        viewModelScope.launch(reportOnly) { avatarCache.warm() }   // best effort
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A base ViewModel that wraps every launch with catch (e: Throwable).
  • Setting loading = false only on the success path, which leaves the spinner on forever after an error or a cancellation.
  • Showing the raw e.message to users. It leaks server internals and isn't localized.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you add a handler to viewModelScope itself? → Not directly. It's created by the library without one. You can pass a handler per launch, or own a custom scope (the closeable-scope patterns are in C7).
  2. Where do 401s go? → Not into each screen. An auth layer (interceptor or authenticator) handles refresh, and the screen sees only Unauthorized once refresh fails.
  3. How do you test this? → A fake use case returning each outcome, runTest with a test Main dispatcher, and assertions on state.value. Plus one test with a throwing fake that checks it propagates (it should crash the test, which proves you didn't swallow bugs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people describe try/catch in each launch, or a global handler. The senior states viewModelScope's composition, splits expected from unexpected failures across layers, keeps errors as state, uses report-only handlers for best-effort work, and explains why a global catch-all makes crash metrics lie.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that put a catch-all in a BaseViewModel usually find out months later that their crash-free rate is meaningless and that dozens of screens show "Something went wrong" for what are actually code bugs.

questions.promptHtml: Should suspend functions in your data layer throw exceptions or return Result/sealed types? What's wrong with using kotlin.Result and runCatching everywhere?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's an architecture question with coroutine-specific traps. Seniors are expected to take a position and defend it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use exceptions for things the caller can't reasonably handle (programmer errors, broken invariants) and typed results for expected outcomes the caller has to handle: offline, not found, validation, unauthorized. A sealed type with domain-specific cases beats kotlin.Result<T>, because Result erases the error to Throwable, so callers can't exhaustively when on it. And runCatching catches Throwable, including CancellationException, so used around suspend calls it breaks cancellation and also wraps genuine bugs as "failures."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Exceptions in coroutines fit structured concurrency well: a failure in one child automatically cancels the related work and comes back through coroutineScope. For "the whole operation is invalid," that's exactly right.
  • Typed results turn expected failures into data, which helps in three places:
    • Exhaustiveness: adding PaymentResult.RequiresOtp makes every when stop compiling until it's handled.
    • Composition with Flow/StateFlow: an outcome can be emitted. An exception terminates the flow (F6).
    • Partial success: List<UploadResult> from a supervised fan-out (Q401).
  • kotlin.Result specifics: since Kotlin 1.5 it's allowed as a return type. It's a value class over Any? (it boxes when used generically). The failure type is always Throwable, and runCatching catches all Throwables.
  • The cancellation hole:
viewModelScope.launch {
    val r = runCatching { repo.load() }   // user leaves screen -> CancellationException captured
    _state.value = r.fold(::Content, ::Error)  // writes Error state for a dead screen,
    analytics.log(...)                         // continues running suspend calls in a cancelled job
}

The next suspend call in a cancelled coroutine throws again, so it usually ends soon anyway. But code between suspension points runs, and you report false "errors."

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface LoginResult {
    data class Success(val session: Session) : LoginResult
    data object InvalidCredentials : LoginResult
    data object Offline : LoginResult
    data class Locked(val retryAfterSeconds: Int) : LoginResult
}

suspend fun login(u: String, p: String): LoginResult = try {
    LoginResult.Success(api.login(u, p))
} catch (e: HttpException) {
    when (e.code()) {
        401 -> LoginResult.InvalidCredentials
        423 -> LoginResult.Locked(e.response()?.headers()?.get("Retry-After")?.toIntOrNull() ?: 60)
        else -> throw e           // unexpected: let it surface
    }
} catch (e: IOException) {
    LoginResult.Offline
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Result<T> everywhere, then getOrNull() at each call site, so errors become nulls with no trace.
  • Wrapping in the repository and catching again in the ViewModel, so nobody knows which layer owns the policy.
  • Typed results that still include data class Unknown(val e: Throwable) as a dumping ground, used for NPEs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is there a cancellation-safe runCatching? → Not in the standard library. Write one that rethrows CancellationException (and arguably Error) and catches the rest.
  2. How do typed results and coroutineScope fail-fast interact? → Results don't cancel siblings. If one branch's failure should abort the others, throw (or convert to an exception) inside the scope.
  3. Arrow's Either/Raise? → A legitimate choice for typed errors with less boilerplate. The trade-off is a dependency and team familiarity. The cancellation rules still apply.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "Result is cleaner." The senior separates expected from unexpected, explains why kotlin.Result loses the error type, shows the runCatching cancellation hole, and keeps fail-fast exceptions where structured concurrency should cancel siblings.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A codebase-wide runCatching around repository calls showed thousands of "errors" in analytics that were really users leaving screens, which masked a real 5xx spike for a day.

questions.contextHtml:
A home dashboard loads 4 sections in parallel. Last sprint, to "fix crashes" (an HttpException fatal at 0.3%), a developer rewrote it as below. Crashes dropped to 0. Two weeks later product reports that ~7% of home loads show at least one blank section, recommendation click-through fell 11%, and support tickets say "home is empty after I come back to the app." No new crashes, no error logs. Backend dashboards show /recs p95 rising from 400 ms to 2.8 s at peak, with 4% 5xx. A red herring: an OkHttp upgrade went out in the same release.

fun loadHome() = viewModelScope.launch {
    supervisorScope {
        val header = async { repo.header() }
        val recs = async { repo.recommendations() }
        val promos = async { repo.promos() }
        val recent = async { repo.recent() }
        _state.value = HomeState(
            header = runCatching { header.await() }.getOrNull(),
            recs = runCatching { recs.await() }.getOrNull(),
            promos = runCatching { promos.await() }.getOrNull(),
            recent = runCatching { recent.await() }.getOrNull(),
        )
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, and how would you fix it so it neither crashes nor fails silently?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the OkHttp upgrade" or "add a retry." Neither explains the blank sections, which are a consequence of the code's design, not of the network.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which section is blank? If it's mostly recs, that matches the backend's 5xx and latency.
    • Is a blank section shown as "empty" or as "error with retry"? It's currently impossible to tell.
    • What does "come back to the app" do: re-call loadHome() from onStart? That matters for cancellation.
    • Are there timeouts configured on these calls?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add non-fatal logging inside the failure branch (server-side config or a quick release), so the actual causes become visible. Check whether the backend /recs regression can be fixed or put behind a cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) /recs 5xx/timeouts are converted into null by getOrNull(), so it renders as an empty section with no log. This matches the 4% 5xx and the sections that are mostly blank.
    • (b) runCatching captures CancellationException: if loadHome() is called again or the user leaves, await() throws cancellation, it's turned into null, and a state with nulls is written. That could explain "empty after returning," if a second load cancels or races the first.
    • (c) The OkHttp upgrade changed timeout defaults. Unlikely: defaults didn't change, and it wouldn't produce section-specific blanks. Check quickly and drop it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Temporary logging of exceptionOrNull() per section with its class name, broken down by section. A unit test with a fake repo where recs throws HttpException(503) shows a null-but-no-error state. A test that calls loadHome() twice with StandardTestDispatcher and checks whether cancellation produces nulls. For (c), compare OkHttp callTimeout/readTimeout config in the two releases.
  5. Root cause: The rewrite fixed a crash by making all failures look like "no data." It removed the signal (no crash and no log) and the UX (no error or retry state). It also turned cancellation into data.
  6. Fix:
sealed interface Section<out T> {
    data object Loading : Section<Nothing>
    data class Ready<T>(val data: T) : Section<T>
    data class Failed(val reason: UiError) : Section<Nothing>
}

private suspend fun <T> loadSection(name: String, block: suspend () -> T): Section<T> = try {
    Section.Ready(block())
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: IOException) {
    Section.Failed(UiError.Offline)
} catch (e: HttpException) {
    Reporter.nonFatal(e, "home_section_$name")
    Section.Failed(UiError.Server)
}

private var homeJob: Job? = null
fun loadHome() {
    homeJob?.cancel()
    homeJob = viewModelScope.launch {
        launch { _state.update { it.copy(header = loadSection("header") { repo.header() }) } }
        launch { _state.update { it.copy(recs = loadSection("recs") { repo.recommendations() }) } }
        launch { _state.update { it.copy(promos = loadSection("promos") { repo.promos() }) } }
        launch { _state.update { it.copy(recent = loadSection("recent") { repo.recent() }) } }
    }
}

Each section fails independently and visibly (error tile with retry). Each one renders as soon as it's ready instead of waiting for the slowest (recs at 2.8 s held back all four). Cancellation still cancels. Unexpected exceptions (an NPE) still propagate and crash, which is what I want. 7. Prevention: A detekt rule banning runCatching around suspend calls in the presentation and data layers. A dashboard metric for "section error rate" per section. A review checklist question: "Does this change turn a failure into absence of data?" 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't put back the original fail-fast coroutineScope, since one section's outage shouldn't blank the home screen. I wouldn't add a global CEH to catch everything. I'd also not jump to retries before the per-section error state exists, because retries without visibility amplify the backend load.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why plain launch children instead of supervisorScope + async? → No values are combined, so each section writes its own state. A child failure that isn't one of my mapped exceptions should take down the load (it's a bug), and update makes the concurrent writes atomic.
  • Should header failure fail the whole screen? → Ask product. If yes, load header first or make its failure a screen-level error. The point is that the policy is explicit.
  • Won't _state.update from 4 coroutines race? → They're all on Main.immediate, and update is a CAS loop anyway, so it's safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: I've reviewed "crash fixes" that were really "visibility removals." Crashes dropped to zero, and so did any way to see the outage. The rule I use: every catch must either produce a user-visible state or a log, ideally both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames OkHttp or suggests retry; doesn't see getOrNull as the issue.
  • Hire: identifies silent swallowing and cancellation capture; proposes per-section error state.
  • Strong hire: adds progressive rendering, keeps bugs crashing, preserves cancellation, adds per-section metrics and a lint rule, and pushes the partial-failure policy back to product.

questions.contextHtml:
A ConfigRepository (Hilt @Singleton) deduplicates concurrent config fetches so 3 screens opening at once don't fire 3 requests. Since this shipped, ~1.5% of sessions see an endless spinner on the Settings screen. No crash, no ANR, no error log. It happens mostly when users open Settings right after backing out of Home. Retrying (reopening Settings) fixes it. A red herring: the config endpoint had a 30-minute outage on the same day the bug was first reported.

@Singleton
class ConfigRepository @Inject constructor(private val api: ConfigApi) {
    private var inFlight: Deferred<Config>? = null

    suspend fun config(): Config = coroutineScope {
        val existing = inFlight
        if (existing != null && existing.isActive) return@coroutineScope existing.await()
        val d = async { api.fetchConfig() }
        inFlight = d
        d.await()
    }
}

class SettingsViewModel(repo: ConfigRepository) : ViewModel() {
    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = Loading
            _state.value = Ready(repo.config())  // spinner forever for some users
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the endless spinner and fix the dedup.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The network hung, add a timeout." A timeout masks the problem. The coroutine isn't stuck at all; it has ended silently.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the spinner frozen while the Settings coroutine is still alive, or is the coroutine gone? (That tells "stuck" apart from "ended.")
    • Does Home also call config()?
    • Is there any invokeOnCompletion or log around the Settings launch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: In Settings, treat a CancellationException from config() while the screen is still active as a failure: show retry. That's a one-line ensureActive check in a hotfix, while the real fix comes in the repository.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The shared Deferred is a child of the first caller's coroutineScope. Home called first, so the async belongs to Home's viewModelScope chain. When the user backs out of Home, it's cancelled. Settings is awaiting that same Deferred, so await() throws CancellationException into Settings' coroutine. Settings' launch completes as "cancelled," which reports nothing and doesn't crash, and _state stays at Loading.
    • (b) The endpoint outage left a hung request. Unlikely: the reopen fixes it, and it's correlated with backing out of Home.
    • (c) A race on the inFlight field. Real (no synchronization), but it causes duplicate fetches, not spinners.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add invokeOnCompletion { cause -> Log.d(...) } on the Settings job. It'll show JobCancellationException while the ViewModel is alive. A unit test: start caller A in scope A, start caller B in scope B, cancel scope A, and assert B gets a CancellationException with B still active.
  5. Root cause: Shared work was owned by an arbitrary caller's scope, and because of the cancellation-is-not-failure rule, the second caller died silently instead of failing loudly.
  6. Fix:
@Singleton
class ConfigRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: ConfigApi,
    @ApplicationScope private val appScope: CoroutineScope,   // SupervisorJob-based, app-lifetime
) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private var inFlight: Deferred<Config>? = null

    suspend fun config(): Config {
        val d = mutex.withLock {
            inFlight?.takeIf { it.isActive } ?: appScope.async { api.fetchConfig() }.also { inFlight = it }
        }
        return d.await()   // a caller leaving cancels only its await, not the shared fetch
    }
}

The fetch now belongs to the app scope, so no single screen can cancel it for the others. If the fetch fails, await() rethrows the real exception (IOException) to every waiter, which they map to an error state. The async is under a SupervisorJob and is always awaited by at least the first caller, so the failure isn't lost silently. The Mutex fixes the race (C8). 7. Prevention: A review rule that shared or cached Deferreds must be created in an owned long-lived scope, never inside a caller's coroutineScope. A test for "caller A cancelled, caller B still gets result." invokeOnCompletion logging of unexpected cancellations on screen-load jobs. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No timeout as the fix; it hides the problem and adds a new failure mode. I wouldn't use GlobalScope (unowned, untestable). I'd also note that the app-scoped fetch keeps running when everyone leaves. For config that's fine; for expensive work I'd reference-count waiters or use shareIn with WhileSubscribed (F5).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the app-scoped fetch fails and nobody awaits it? → The first caller always awaits, so it's surfaced. If all callers leave first, it sits in a Deferred that's dropped on the next call. Acceptable, but log it via invokeOnCompletion.
  • Could NonCancellable around the await help? → No. It would keep Settings waiting even when Settings itself is being cancelled, so it breaks Settings' own cancellation.
  • Should failures be cached? → No. Clear inFlight on failure so the next call retries. isActive being false on a failed Deferred already gives you that.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "request coalescing" helper caused intermittent infinite spinners for months because the shared Deferred lived in whichever scope asked first. The tell was that the bug only happened when navigating quickly between two screens that needed the same data.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a timeout; doesn't realize the coroutine ended.
  • Hire: explains that await on a cancelled Deferred throws CancellationException and silently ends the awaiter; moves ownership to an app scope.
  • Strong hire: adds the mutex, describes failure fan-out to all waiters, writes the two-scope cancellation test, and discusses when the shared work should stop.

questions.promptHtml: What happens when an exception is thrown during exception handling: inside a finally block, inside an invokeOnCompletion handler, or inside a CoroutineExceptionHandler itself?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are the edge cases that produce confusing crash reports. Knowing them is a sign you've debugged real failures, not just read the docs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There are three different behaviors. A finally that throws replaces the original exception under normal Kotlin/JVM rules; it isn't automatically suppressed onto it. However, if the coroutine is already failing and a child's cleanup throws, the Job collects it as a suppressed exception. A throwing invokeOnCompletion handler is wrapped in CompletionHandlerException and sent to the coroutine exception-handling path. A CoroutineExceptionHandler that throws gets wrapped together with the original into a RuntimeException that goes to the thread's uncaught handler, so you crash after all.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1) finally in the SAME coroutine body
   try { throw IOException("A") } finally { throw IllegalStateException("B") }
   -> coroutine fails with B; A is LOST (plain JVM semantics, unless you addSuppressed manually)

2) finally in a CHILD while the parent is already failing with A
   parent collects child's B -> B added as suppressed on A (Q387)

3) invokeOnCompletion { throw X }
   -> CompletionHandlerException("Exception in completion handler ... for <job>", X)
   -> handleCoroutineException(context, it) -> CEH or thread handler (crash on Android)

4) CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> throw Y }
   -> library catches Y, builds RuntimeException("Exception while trying to handle coroutine exception", Y)
      with original e added as suppressed (when they differ)
   -> passed to the uncaught-exception path -> crash on Android

Also, a finally that calls a suspend function in a cancelled coroutine throws CancellationException at that suspension, which also replaces the original exception. That's another reason cleanup that must suspend goes in withContext(NonCancellable) (mechanics in C5).

Hidden-original cases to watch for:

  • use {} on Closeable: Kotlin's use does add the close exception as suppressed (it calls addSuppressed on Java 7+ targets), so the original survives. A hand-written try/finally doesn't.
  • Logging in finally that throws (for example, a formatting NPE) hides the real failure.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: cleanup failure replaces the real cause
scope.launch {
    val tx = db.begin()
    try {
        tx.write(data)          // throws SQLiteConstraintException (the real bug)
    } finally {
        tx.close()              // throws IllegalStateException("already closed") -> this is what you see
    }
}

// Better: preserve the primary failure
scope.launch {
    val tx = db.begin()
    var primary: Throwable? = null
    try {
        tx.write(data)
    } catch (t: Throwable) {
        primary = t
        throw t
    } finally {
        try {
            tx.close()
        } catch (closeError: Throwable) {
            if (primary != null) primary.addSuppressed(closeError) else throw closeError
        }
    }
}
// Simplest when the type is Closeable: tx.use { it.write(data) }

// Handler that must never throw
val safeHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
    runCatching { reporter.nonFatal(e) }   // ok here: no suspension, nothing to cancel
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Network calls or launching coroutines in a CEH. The reporter can throw or recurse.
  • Heavy work in invokeOnCompletion. It runs synchronously on the completing thread, possibly main.
  • Assuming the top exception in a crash is the root cause. When finally replaced it, it isn't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does CompletionHandlerException crash the app? → If it reaches the uncaught path with no handler, yes.
  2. Why doesn't Kotlin suppress automatically in try/finally? → It follows Java semantics. Only try-with-resources (Java) and use (Kotlin) add suppressed exceptions.
  3. Can a CEH safely call launch? → Technically yes, but the scope may be cancelled, and recursive failures can loop. Prefer posting to a bounded, non-coroutine reporting queue.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people know finally always runs. The senior knows the four distinct outcomes, which ones lose the original, how use differs from try/finally, and makes handlers and completion callbacks non-throwing by design.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster titled "IllegalStateException: cursor already closed" turned out to be a masked SQLiteDatabaseLockedException. The fix was in the transaction code, not the cursor code.

questions.subtopic: Internals of exception routing in the Job tree
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how kotlinx.coroutines decides, internally, who handles a failed coroutine's exception. What are childCancelled, handlesException, and scoped coroutines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level interviewers like to check that your rules come from the mechanism, so you can reason about unfamiliar builders and custom scopes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When a coroutine finishes with an exception, JobSupport picks a root cause from the collected exceptions, then asks two questions. First, cancelParent(cause): scoped coroutines return true straight away (they'll rethrow to the caller), cancellation exceptions count as handled, and otherwise it calls parent.childCancelled(cause), which a supervisor answers with false and a regular coroutine answers with true. Second, if the parent didn't take it, handleJobException(cause) runs. launch overrides it to call the CEH or the uncaught handler, async doesn't override it, so the exception stays in its state. A root Job() cancels itself but reports "not handled," because its handlesException is false when it has no handling parent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A simplified view (actual code is in JobSupport.kt; names are accurate, bodies abbreviated):

finalizeFinishingState(state, proposedUpdate):
    finalException = getFinalRootCause(exceptions)          // first non-CancellationException, else first
    addSuppressedExceptions(finalException, exceptions)     // the rest, skipping cancellations
    if (finalException != null && !isCancellation(finalException)):
        handled = cancelParent(finalException) || handleJobException(finalException)
        if (handled) mark exception as handled

cancelParent(cause):
    if (isScopedCoroutine) return true                      // coroutineScope, withContext, runBlocking...
    isCancellation = cause is CancellationException
    parent = parentHandle
    if (parent == null) return isCancellation
    return parent.childCancelled(cause) || isCancellation

JobSupport.childCancelled(cause):                           // called on the PARENT
    if (cause is CancellationException) return true
    return cancelImpl(cause) && handlesException

SupervisorJobImpl.childCancelled(cause) = false             // never take responsibility

handleJobException(e):
    JobSupport default        -> false                      // async/Deferred: keep in state
    StandaloneCoroutine (launch), ActorCoroutine -> handleCoroutineException(context, e); true

Reading it:

  • Regular parent coroutine: cancelImpl cancels it (and so all siblings), handlesException is true for coroutines, so the child is "handled." The exception then goes to the parent's own finalization.
  • Root Job() / CoroutineScope(Job()): JobImpl.handlesException is true only if some ancestor handles exceptions. At the root it's false. So the scope is cancelled and the child's own handleJobException runs. That's why CoroutineScope(Job() + handler) both calls the handler and kills the scope.
  • Scoped coroutines answer true in cancelParent, so the parent isn't touched. Their result (an exception) resumes the caller's continuation, which rethrows it.
  • async under a supervisor: the parent says false, handleJobException says false, so the exception is "unhandled but stored." That's the silent-loss case.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Predict the output using the rules above
fun main() = runBlocking {
    val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> println("handler: ${e.message}") }
    val scope = CoroutineScope(Job() + handler)
    val a = scope.launch { delay(50); println("A done") }
    scope.launch { throw IllegalStateException("B failed") }
    delay(100)
    println("scope active=${scope.isActive}, A cancelled=${a.isCancelled}")
    scope.launch { println("C never runs") }   // scope already cancelled
    delay(50)
}
// handler: B failed
// scope active=false, A cancelled=true

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating "root" as "launched from a scope" and missing the Job() vs SupervisorJob() difference in how the scope survives.
  • Thinking async has an override that crashes. It never reports uncaught.
  • Relying on internal function names in production code. They're internal and can change between versions. Use them for reasoning only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you build a custom builder that reports uncaught like launch? → Extend AbstractCoroutine and override handleJobException. That's an internal-ish API (@InternalCoroutinesApi in places), so wrap launch instead in app code.
  2. Why does runBlocking rethrow child failures? → Its coroutine is scoped-like: its result is the block's outcome, which it rethrows to the blocking caller.
  3. What does cancelImpl do with a CancellationException from a child? → Nothing to the parent. childCancelled returns true early, so the child "handled" it by being cancelled.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people give the rules. The senior gives the algorithm (root-cause selection, cancelParent, childCancelled, handlesException, handleJobException) and derives every rule from it, including the Job() scope case.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team couldn't explain why their CoroutineScope(Job() + handler) sync manager "stopped working after the first error" even though the handler fired. Tracing childCancelled showed the scope Job had been cancelled.

questions.subtopic: Scope with Job() dies after first failure
questions.promptHtml: You build CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + handler) for a long-lived manager and one launch throws. The handler logs it, but later launch calls do nothing. What happened, and how do you build a scope that survives child failures?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the root-cause of the "manager stops working after the first error" class of bugs. It tests whether you know a handler doesn't keep the scope alive, and whether you know what CoroutineScope(...) adds to the context.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CoroutineScope(context) adds a plain Job() if the context has no Job. A plain Job is a regular parent: a child's failure cancels it and therefore every sibling. The handler fires because that child was the top of the chain, but the scope's Job is now Cancelled, and launch on a cancelled scope returns a Job that's already cancelled and never runs the body, with no error. The fix is SupervisorJob() in the scope's context, plus a handler or try/catch for the children, since supervision stops propagation but doesn't make failures disappear.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• fun CoroutineScope(context) returns ContextScope(if (context[Job] != null) context else context + Job()). So you always have a Job in a scope made this way.
  • With Job(): child fails, childCancelled returns true, so the scope Job moves to Cancelled. Siblings get CancellationException. New children created after that start already cancelled. (Q396 has the algorithm.)
  • With SupervisorJob(): childCancelled returns false, so the scope stays Active. The failed child handles its own exception: its CEH or the thread's uncaught handler.
  • The silence is the nasty part. launch on a cancelled scope doesn't throw. The block just never executes. Nothing is logged.
CoroutineScope(Job() + handler)           CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler)
  launch A ─┐                               launch A ─┐
  launch B ─┤ B throws                      launch B ─┤ B throws
  handler(B) fired                          handler(B) fired
  scope Job: Cancelled                      scope Job: Active
  A: cancelled                              A: keeps running
  launch C: silently never runs             launch C: runs

Choose the lifecycle on purpose:

  • Scope that must outlive failures (app-level, a manager): SupervisorJob() + handler.
  • Scope where one failure should abort the unit (a single operation): scoped builders (coroutineScope) and let the exception propagate.
  • Always keep a handle to cancel the scope when the owner dies (scope.cancel() in close()/onCleared()).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncManager(api: Api) {
    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> Reporter.nonFatal(e) }

    // Broken: first failure disables the manager forever
    private val brokenScope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + handler)

    // Correct
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)

    fun sync(item: Item) = scope.launch { api.push(item) }

    fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

// Cheap guard in tests / debug builds
fun CoroutineScope.requireActive() = check(coroutineContext.isActive) { "scope is cancelled; launch is a no-op" }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing the handler "handles" the failure and the scope carries on.
  • launch(SupervisorJob()) per call. That detaches from the scope (C4 owns that bug) and isn't the fix.
  • A supervisor scope without a handler: children still crash the app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect a dead scope at runtime? → scope.isActive / coroutineContext.job.isCancelled. Log it in debug builds, and in a manager's entry points check it and fail loudly.
  2. Should a manager restart its scope after a fatal failure? → Rarely. Better to make children handle expected failures, and let genuine bugs crash so they're visible.
  3. Does viewModelScope have this problem? → No, it uses SupervisorJob. A hand-made CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main) in a custom class does.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE: "use SupervisorJob." The senior explains that CoroutineScope() injects Job(), why the silent no-op happens, and ties the decision to ownership and lifecycle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background uploader stopped uploading after the first SocketTimeoutException each session. The handler logged it, so dashboards looked fine, while the queue grew until the app was killed.

questions.contextHtml:
Eight months ago a platform team added BaseViewModel.launchSafe to "end coroutine crashes." Adoption: 140 call sites. Today's incident: for 36 hours, 9% of checkout attempts silently failed (spinner, then the screen returned to the cart with a generic "Something went wrong"). Crash-free sessions stayed at 99.96% the whole time, so no alert fired. Root cause was found by support: a backend change returned a new JSON field type, and a SerializationException in the checkout response was caught by launchSafe. Another symptom found in the review: the app sometimes continued to show "Order placed" after the user had navigated away. A red herring: the payment gateway had a short latency blip the same week.

abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel() {
    protected val _error = MutableSharedFlow<String>(extraBufferCapacity = 1)
    val error = _error.asSharedFlow()

    protected fun launchSafe(block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit) = viewModelScope.launch {
        try {
            block()
        } catch (e: Throwable) {
            _error.tryEmit("Something went wrong")
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: You're leading the post-incident review. What went wrong, what do you change, and how do you prevent this class of failure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add logging to the catch block." That's a good step, but it keeps the design: every failure of every kind, including bugs and cancellation, becomes one generic message.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Why did nobody see it for 36 hours? Which alerts depend on crashes?
    • Did the "Order placed" message come from the launchSafe path, and what exactly happened on navigation?
    • Is there any test that exercises a throwing use case through a ViewModel?
    • Who owns BaseViewModel and what's the review process for changes to it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the DTO to tolerate the new field type (or roll back the backend change). Ship a hotfix that logs e in launchSafe as non-fatal with the call-site name, so we can finally see the other failures this wrapper is hiding.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) catch (e: Throwable) swallowed a bug-class exception (SerializationException) and reduced it to a toast-like message with no log and no metric. This is the incident.
    • (b) The same catch swallowed CancellationException when the user navigated away: the catch ran, emitted an error, and the code after block() kept running its own logic. That explains the stale "Order placed."
    • (c) MutableSharedFlow with tryEmit and no replay lost errors when nobody was collecting, such as while the app was backgrounded (F2b covers event semantics).
    • (d) The gateway latency blip. Real, but it shows up as timeouts, which a retry state would explain, not a 9% steady failure.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pull the 140 call sites by usage and group them by what they call. Reproduce (a) in a unit test with a fake use case throwing SerializationException: the test passes silently, which is the bug. For (b), a test that cancels viewModelScope mid-call and asserts the error flow didn't emit. For (c), check collectors with a debug log on the error flow.
  5. Root cause: A single abstraction decided policy for all failure types. It removed the crash signal without replacing it with another signal. It also broke cancellation by catching Throwable.
  6. Fix:
protected fun launchSafe(
    tag: String,
    onExpected: (Throwable) -> Unit,
    block: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit,
) = viewModelScope.launch {
    try {
        block()
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e                                             // never swallow
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        onExpected(e)                                       // expected: caller maps it to state
    } catch (e: HttpException) {
        Reporter.nonFatal(e, tag)                           // visible in metrics
        onExpected(e)
    }
    // anything else (bugs, SerializationException) propagates and crashes, so we see it
}

Long term, deprecate launchSafe in favour of explicit try/catch in new code (or typed results from the data layer), and introduce a contract test per ViewModel: "unexpected exception propagates." 7. Prevention: (i) A business-level alert on checkout success rate, not just crash-free sessions. (ii) A detekt rule: catch (e: Throwable) or catch (e: Exception) without a CancellationException branch or rethrow fails CI. (iii) Contract-change monitoring: server-driven schema tests plus ignoreUnknownKeys/coercion settings decided on purpose. (iv) Shared infrastructure changes need a design review that lists what the abstraction hides. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't revert to raw launches with no handling at all. Some failures are expected and users deserve a message. I wouldn't turn off crash-on-bug because the product team likes the crash-free number. A lower crash-free rate with a visible bug is cheaper than a hidden 9% revenue loss.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership wants crash-free sessions kept above 99.9%. How do you respond? → Separate "crash-free" from "failure-free" and show the incident as the cost of optimizing the first. Offer non-fatal tracking with an alert budget so bugs are visible without crashing.
  • Can we keep catching Exception but report it? → Yes, if every unexpected exception is reported with a tag and the user sees an accurate "unexpected error" state. It's still worse than crashing in dev builds, where I'd rethrow.
  • How do you migrate 140 call sites? → Codemod to the new signature with a default onExpected that preserves the old message, then triage by call site, starting with money paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Every platform team I've seen build a "safe launch" wrapper has a version of this incident in its future. The wrapper looks like hygiene until a bug-class exception lands on a revenue path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only logging or blames the backend.
  • Hire: identifies catch-all + cancellation swallowing; splits expected from unexpected; reports with tags.
  • Strong hire: adds product-level monitoring, lint rule, migration plan, and discusses the crash-free-rate incentive problem.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (2M DAU) syncs unsent messages with a SyncScope. After a release, backend SRE reports request spikes to /messages/send: 6x normal volume during a 20-minute regional degradation, then the API's rate limiter starts returning 429 and the spike continues for 40 more minutes. Devices on bad networks show battery drain in vitals. Crashlytics shows nothing. The release note: "automatic retry for failed syncs." A red herring: a CDN change shipped the same day.

object SyncScope {
    private val handler: CoroutineExceptionHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e ->
        Reporter.nonFatal(e)
        scope.launch { sync() }          // "retry"
    }
    val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)

    fun sync() = scope.launch {
        outbox.pending().forEach { api.send(it) }   // throws IOException on bad network
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the traffic pattern and rewrite the retry so it's safe.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a delay before the retry." Better than nothing, but it keeps retry in a handler (after death, unbounded, untracked), and doesn't address idempotency or the 429s.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is sync() also triggered by connectivity callbacks or app foreground events? Those multiply the loops.
    • Does /messages/send accept an idempotency key? Duplicate messages are the other half of this incident.
    • What does the outbox do with items that permanently fail (4xx)?
    • Is there a max age for a pending message?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side: rate limit by device and return Retry-After. Client: a remote kill switch or a flag that disables the handler retry. Ship a hotfix that removes scope.launch { sync() } from the handler (it's one line) and lets the next trigger (connectivity, foreground) start a sync.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The handler relaunches sync() immediately on each failure: unbounded, zero-delay loop for any device with a failing network. Each loop iteration is a request, which explains the 6x multiplier. This is the cause.
    • (b) The loop restarts each failing item from the head of the outbox (forEach fails on the first), so it's hammering the same message. That would produce the same-endpoint pattern.
    • (c) 429 handling: api.send throws HttpException(429) and the handler retries instantly, so the rate limiter makes it worse. A feedback loop.
    • (d) CDN change. The traffic is on an API endpoint behind no cache. Unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify each: Request logs grouped by device ID and interval (the same device sending every ~50 ms confirms the loop). A local reproduction with a fake API that throws and a virtual-time test counting calls over 60 seconds (runTest, advanceTimeBy). Battery vitals matching devices with the failing call.
  5. Root cause: Retry logic placed in a CoroutineExceptionHandler, which has no attempt count, no delay, no knowledge of the failure type, and no cancellation story. A failure produced another launch, whose failure produced another, forever.
  6. Fix:
class OutboxSyncer(
    private val api: Api, private val outbox: Outbox,
    private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val clock: Clock,
) {
    private val running = AtomicBoolean(false)

    fun trigger() {
        if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return           // single flight
        scope.launch {
            try { drain() } finally { running.set(false) }
        }
    }

    private suspend fun drain() {
        var attempt = 0
        while (true) {
            val msg = outbox.next() ?: return
            try {
                api.send(msg, idempotencyKey = msg.id)
                outbox.markSent(msg); attempt = 0
            } catch (e: HttpException) {
                when {
                    e.code() == 429 -> delay(retryAfter(e) ?: backoff(attempt++))
                    e.code() in 400..499 -> outbox.markFailed(msg)       // permanent
                    else -> delay(backoff(attempt++))
                }
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                if (attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) return                      // wait for next trigger (connectivity)
                delay(backoff(attempt++))
            }
        }
    }
    private fun backoff(n: Int): Long = (1_000L shl n.coerceAtMost(6)).coerceAtMost(60_000) + Random.nextLong(500)
}

Retry now has bounded attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, Retry-After respect, permanent-failure classification, single flight, and an idempotency key. On long outages it stops and waits for a connectivity trigger or a WorkManager job. 7. Prevention: A virtual-time test: "N consecutive failures produce at most M requests in T seconds." A lint/review rule that handlers only report. Client-side request-rate telemetry per endpoint and a canary release with a request-volume guard. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't rely on the server rate limit alone. I wouldn't use unbounded retry for user-visible sends: after a limit, show "failed, tap to retry." I'd also not build my own durable scheduler here. When the app is in the background and has to retry for hours, WorkManager is the right tool (C7 covers it).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not retry {} on a Flow? → Fine for stream sources (F6). This is a queue drain with per-item policy, so an explicit loop is clearer.
  • Is AtomicBoolean enough for single flight? → For one-process use, yes. It's a guard against re-entry, not data sharing (C8 has Mutex alternatives).
  • What if the process dies mid-send? → The idempotency key plus an outbox marking after success makes at-least-once delivery safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: I've seen a retry-in-handler change take down a rate limiter that protected the whole API. The change looked like a one-liner, which is exactly why it passed review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a fixed delay in the handler.
  • Hire: moves retry to explicit logic with bounded backoff and error classification.
  • Strong hire: adds jitter, Retry-After, idempotency, single-flight, a virtual-time test, and a fleet-level safety net.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design the exception types that flow through repository, domain and ViewModel layers in a coroutine-based app? What rules do you set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you can set team conventions that keep error handling consistent and cancellation-safe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The data layer converts library exceptions (HttpException, SQLiteException, SerializationException) into a small set of domain types at the boundary, keeping the original as cause. Expected failures are modelled as sealed result types or a sealed exception hierarchy under Exception. Unexpected ones aren't converted. Rules: never extend CancellationException, always pass cause, don't leak transport types upward, and map to user-facing text only in the UI layer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Boundary mapping. Retrofit/Room types shouldn't appear in ViewModel code. The repository maps them once: HttpException(401) becomes AuthExpired, IOException becomes Offline, and so on. Then changing the HTTP client doesn't touch UI code.
  • Sealed hierarchy example:
Exception
 └─ DomainException (sealed)
      ├─ Offline
      ├─ Unauthorized
      ├─ NotFound(resource)
      ├─ Conflict(serverVersion)
      └─ ServerError(code)

A sealed hierarchy gives the compiler exhaustiveness at catch sites that use when (e).

  • Which to catch vs let through. Expected business failures get mapped. Bugs (NullPointerException, IllegalStateException) aren't wrapped, since wrapping them into DomainException.Unknown just relabels a bug as an operational failure.
  • Cause chain. throw ServerError(code, cause = e) keeps the stack for Crashlytics and debugging. Without cause, you only see the mapping site.
  • Never extend CancellationException (Q386). The compiler lets you; the runtime then treats your domain failure as a normal stop.
  • Stack trace cost. Exceptions fill their stack trace on construction, which is a measurable cost in hot paths, but not for HTTP failures. If you use exceptions for control flow in a tight loop, prefer results.
  • Presentation. Map DomainException to UiError (string resources, retry affordances) in the ViewModel or a mapper. Don't embed Android Context/strings in the domain layer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed class DomainException(message: String?, cause: Throwable? = null) : Exception(message, cause) {
    class Offline(cause: Throwable) : DomainException("offline", cause)
    class Unauthorized(cause: Throwable) : DomainException("unauthorized", cause)
    class ServerError(val code: Int, cause: Throwable) : DomainException("server $code", cause)
}

suspend fun <T> mapErrors(block: suspend () -> T): T = try {
    block()
} catch (e: IOException) {
    throw DomainException.Offline(e)
} catch (e: HttpException) {
    throw if (e.code() == 401) DomainException.Unauthorized(e) else DomainException.ServerError(e.code(), e)
}   // CancellationException passes through untouched; unknown exceptions pass through too

fun DomainException.toUi(): UiError = when (this) {
    is DomainException.Offline -> UiError.Offline
    is DomainException.Unauthorized -> UiError.LoginRequired
    is DomainException.ServerError -> UiError.Server(code)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A mapper using catch (e: Exception) that wraps everything, including cancellation, into Unknown.
  • Dropping cause.
  • Domain layer returning user-visible strings.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Exceptions or sealed results for these domain failures? → Both are valid. Q392 covers the choice. The hierarchy approach suits fail-fast flows; results suit UI branching.
  2. Should the Retrofit interface itself throw domain exceptions? → Map in a repository or call adapter. A custom CallAdapter can do it centrally.
  3. How does this interact with Crashlytics grouping? → Wrapped exceptions group by the new top type, so keep the cause and include a stable message, or you split one issue into many.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: At 3 YOE people catch Exception in ViewModels. The senior has a layered convention: map once at the boundary, preserve cause, stay cancellation-safe, never relabel bugs, and map text at the edge.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app where HttpException leaked into 60 ViewModels needed a month-long refactor when they moved to Ktor, because each ViewModel inspected status codes itself.

questions.contextHtml: A photo-sharing app lets users upload up to 30 photos at once. Product requirements, as written: "Upload all photos in parallel for speed. If some fail, tell the user which ones failed and let them retry just those. Don't fail the batch because one photo is bad. Cancelling the screen should stop the uploads." Current code uses coroutineScope { photos.map { async { upload(it) } }.awaitAll() }. Data from the last month: 12% of batches have at least one failure (mostly >10 MB files hitting a 413, and flaky networks); in those cases users see "Upload failed" and all 30 photos restart. The server enforces 6 concurrent connections per client, and 429s appear when the app opens 30 at once. A red herring: an engineer proposes switching to WorkManager as the fix.
questions.promptHtml: Design the fan-out so partial failure is first-class, and explain how exceptions and cancellation behave.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap each upload in try/catch." That's part of it, but it skips concurrency limits, cancellation, result modelling, and which failures are retryable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Should uploads continue when the app is backgrounded? That's the one case where WorkManager is the right tool, and I'd treat it separately.
    • Which failures are retryable? 413 isn't. Timeouts are.
    • Do we need ordering, or progress per photo?
    • Is the server idempotent per photo ID?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency at 4 (the server's limit is 6, leaving headroom), which should remove most 429s. Convert failures into per-photo results so the user stops losing the whole batch.
  3. Hypotheses (about the current failure experience), ranked:
    • (a) coroutineScope+awaitAll is fail-fast: the first failure cancels the other 29 uploads, which restarts everything. Matches the symptoms.
    • (b) 30 parallel connections trigger 429s, which the code treats as failures, making (a) worse.
    • (c) Large files fail with 413 and are retried again and again, because nothing classifies them as permanent.
  4. How I'd verify each: Server logs for cancelled-connection patterns at the time of failure; a test with a fake uploader where photo #7 throws and a virtual-time check of how many uploads were cancelled; client metrics by status code.
  5. Root cause: The scope semantics don't match the product requirement. The requirement is "independent children, aggregate result," which is a supervisor-style design with explicit result modelling, plus a concurrency limit.
  6. Fix:
sealed interface UploadOutcome {
    data class Done(val id: String) : UploadOutcome
    data class Retryable(val id: String, val cause: Throwable) : UploadOutcome
    data class Rejected(val id: String, val reason: String) : UploadOutcome
}

suspend fun uploadAll(photos: List<Photo>, onProgress: (String, Float) -> Unit): List<UploadOutcome> =
    supervisorScope {                                   // children independent; caller's cancellation still propagates
        val gate = Semaphore(permits = 4)
        photos.map { p ->
            async {
                gate.withPermit {
                    try {
                        api.upload(p, onProgress = { onProgress(p.id, it) })
                        UploadOutcome.Done(p.id)
                    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
                        throw e
                    } catch (e: HttpException) {
                        if (e.code() == 413 || e.code() in 400..499 && e.code() != 429)
                            UploadOutcome.Rejected(p.id, "too large or invalid")
                        else UploadOutcome.Retryable(p.id, e)
                    } catch (e: IOException) {
                        UploadOutcome.Retryable(p.id, e)
                    }
                }
            }
        }.awaitAll()                                    // never throws for expected failures
    }

Exceptions semantics: expected failures are values, so awaitAll doesn't throw and nobody is cancelled. An unexpected exception (a bug) inside one async is stored in its Deferred under the supervisor, but awaitAll rethrows it and the surrounding supervisorScope body fails, which cancels the rest. That's acceptable: bugs should be loud. Cancelling the screen cancels the supervisorScope, which cancels all in-flight uploads, as the requirement says. "Retry only failed" re-calls uploadAll with the Retryable ones. 7. Prevention: A test with a fake API and virtual time: one 413, one timeout, assert that 28 succeed, outcomes are classified, and max concurrency is 4. A test cancelling mid-batch asserts that no uploads continue. Dashboards on per-status upload outcomes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use plain launch + shared mutable list for results (needs synchronization, no aggregation). I wouldn't retry inside this function without backoff and caps (see the retry incident, Q399). WorkManager is a separate decision: it's right if uploads must survive the app being backgrounded or killed; it doesn't address fan-out semantics, which would still need this design inside each worker.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why supervisorScope if no launch child can fail in the scope? → Because an unexpected exception in an async would otherwise cancel siblings immediately instead of when I awaitAll. Either is defensible. I'd choose the supervisor to let all other uploads settle before reporting.
  • What if the user wants to cancel a single photo? → Keep a Map<String, Job> or use per-photo child scopes. Cancellation of one child under a supervisor doesn't affect siblings.
  • Semaphore vs limitedParallelism(4)? → limitedParallelism limits threads, not concurrent suspended calls. Network uploads suspend, so a semaphore bounds the actual in-flight work (C8 owns Semaphore details).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "retry failed uploads" feature was requested three times before someone noticed the real problem was the fail-fast scope cancelling the 29 healthy uploads. The feature was a symptom.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: per-upload try/catch only, or WorkManager as the answer.
  • Hire: supervisor semantics, results as values, concurrency cap, cancellation of the batch.
  • Strong hire: classifies retryable vs permanent, explains where unexpected exceptions go, designs the retry path, and knows when WorkManager is a separate concern.

questions.contextHtml:
You're reviewing a ViewModel before release. It handles a profile edit screen for an app with 800k DAU. QA reports "sometimes the screen shows Saved but the server has no change," "after a failed save, the Save button stays disabled forever," and Crashlytics has a growing non-fatal JobCancellationException count. Find the bugs.

class EditProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(EditUi())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()

    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
        _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(error = e.message)                       // (1)
    }

    init {
        viewModelScope.async(handler) { _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(profile = repo.load()) } // (2)
    }

    fun save(name: String) {
        _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(saving = true)
        try {
            viewModelScope.launch {                                          // (3)
                repo.save(name)
                _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(saved = true)
            }
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(error = e.message)
        }
        _ui.value = _ui.value.copy(saving = false)                           // (4)
    }

    fun autosave(draft: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch(Job()) {                                       // (5)
            try {
                repo.saveDraft(draft)
            } catch (e: Exception) {                                         // (6)
                Reporter.nonFatal(e)
            } finally {
                repo.markDraftSynced()                                       // (7) suspend fun
            }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: List every bug, say what each one does at runtime, and give the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Finding only (3), the try/catch around launch. Missing the cancellation and lifecycle bugs means missing the ones that cause the Crashlytics noise.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is repo.save idempotent? Is markDraftSynced required for correctness? Is saved = true a one-off event or state? Those decide how aggressive the fixes are.
  2. Immediate mitigation: The Saved-but-not-saved report is the most damaging, so I'd fix (3)/(4) first. It's a data-trust issue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (by user impact):
    • (3)+(4): try/catch around launch never catches, and saving = false runs immediately after launch returns, long before the save finishes. The button re-enables while the save is in flight, so double taps happen, and failures never reach the catch. Failures go to the uncaught path (crash) or are lost.
    • Saved-but-not-saved: the error path is never set by a failed save. In a failed run the user can still see "saved" from a previous successful save because saved is never reset.
    • (5): launch(Job()) replaces the parent. The autosave isn't a child of viewModelScope any more, so onCleared() doesn't cancel it. It outlives the ViewModel and holds repo (and maybe the UI state) — a leak. It also means failures in it aren't reported to the ViewModel's scope.
    • (6)+(7): catch (e: Exception) catches CancellationException, so cancellation is reported as a non-fatal error. That's the growing JobCancellationException count. markDraftSynced() is a suspend call in finally: in a cancelled coroutine it throws CancellationException immediately at its first suspension and doesn't run, so cleanup silently doesn't happen when it matters most. It also marks the draft synced even when saveDraft failed.
    • (2): async with a handler. The handler is ignored for async, and nobody awaits, so a load failure vanishes: the screen shows an empty profile and no error. Also, async here should be launch.
    • (1): the handler writes e.message (often null, raw, not localized) into UI state and runs on whatever thread completes the coroutine, which can be a non-main thread. On StateFlow.value that's thread-safe, but the copy-then-set is a read-modify-write race with other writers (use update).
  4. How I'd verify each: runTest with fakes: a throwing repo.save (the test fails with an uncaught exception, which confirms (3)); cancel viewModelScope during autosave and check for a non-fatal report (6) and whether markDraftSynced ran (7); viewModel.onCleared() via a test helper and check whether the autosave job is still active (5); a failing repo.load() and check the state (2). LeakCanary or a heap dump for (5).
  5. Root cause: One mindset error repeated: treating coroutines like callbacks with try/catch outside, handlers as local catches, and finally as always-runs-suspend-safe.
  6. Fix:
class EditProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(EditUi())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {                                              // launch, not async
            try {
                val p = repo.load()
                _ui.update { it.copy(profile = p) }
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                _ui.update { it.copy(error = UiError.Offline) }
            }
        }
    }

    private var saveJob: Job? = null
    fun save(name: String) {
        if (saveJob?.isActive == true) return                                // blocks double taps
        saveJob = viewModelScope.launch {
            _ui.update { it.copy(saving = true, saved = false, error = null) }
            try {
                repo.save(name)
                _ui.update { it.copy(saved = true) }
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                _ui.update { it.copy(error = UiError.Offline) }
            } catch (e: HttpException) {
                _ui.update { it.copy(error = UiError.Server) }
            } finally {
                _ui.update { it.copy(saving = false) }                       // non-suspending: safe in cancellation
            }
        }
    }

    fun autosave(draft: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {                                              // stays a child of the ViewModel
            var ok = false
            try {
                repo.saveDraft(draft)
                ok = true
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                Reporter.nonFatal(e)                                         // expected type only; cancellation passes through
            } finally {
                if (ok) withContext(NonCancellable) { repo.markDraftSynced() }
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Review checklist items: try/catch around launch? async unused? Handler on a child? Job()/SupervisorJob() in a builder call? catch (Exception) around suspend calls? Suspend call in finally? Plus detekt rules for the mechanical ones and a ViewModel test template with a throwing fake.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't keep the NonCancellable cleanup for long operations, since it makes cancellation wait on it. If markDraftSynced is slow or requires the network, it should be an idempotent job in WorkManager instead. I wouldn't fix (1) by attaching more handlers; the right move is to remove the handler and map failures where they happen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• saved = true as state: what about "show a snackbar once"? → That's event delivery (F2b). The state flag has to be consumed or cleared, or it replays on rotation.
  • Is saveJob?.isActive enough against double taps? → On a single (main) thread, yes. For multi-threaded callers use a Mutex or AtomicBoolean (C8).
  • Why Main.immediate matters here? → The update calls before the first suspension run synchronously on main, so saving = true is set before save() returns.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single ViewModel like this once had seven separate error-handling defects, each one looking plausible on its own. They were all variations of two ideas: "exceptions behave like in blocking code" and "handlers behave like catch."

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds only the try/catch-around-launch bug.
  • Hire: finds (2), (3)/(4), (5), (6) and explains each mechanically.
  • Strong hire: finds all seven, including suspend-in-finally and the saved state reset, orders them by user impact, and fixes them without introducing a catch-all.
